This book is a faith-based companion for reflection and practice. It is not medical, mental-health, legal, or addiction-treatment advice, and it does not replace a doctor, therapist, counselor, pastor, or emergency services. The author is not a licensed clinician. Prayer belongs beside — not in place of — treatment, medication, safe housing, and safety planning.

Your safety comes first

If you are in danger, call 911 (or your local emergency number). If you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988 (U.S.). If you are physically dependent on alcohol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates, do not stop suddenly without medical supervision — withdrawal can be dangerous. The resource page at the back of the book lists additional help. Phone numbers and services change; please confirm them before you rely on them.

About the stories and ideas

Personal testimony is shared as lived experience, not as a formula or a promise of any outcome. Interpretations of Scripture are labeled as interpretation and offered for you to test against the Bible and with wise, trusted people. Nothing in this book guarantees healing, deliverance, income, or any particular result.

In memory

In Memory of Brandi Renee · January 27, 1986 – December 17, 2021

You survived. Now we rebuild.

Before day one

Meet Nikki and Big Boy

Hey. I’m Nikki, and this is Big Boy, my battle buddy: a big gray-and-white American Bully with a muscular build and no ears, who stood beside me through some of my loneliest days.

I lost my sister to addiction. I have lived through homelessness, trafficking, abuse, addiction, and a long, destructive relationship. When I reached for help, too often there were strings attached, or a watered-down verse and a pat on the head. I needed somewhere that could hold the truth about trauma without pushing God out of the room.

I am not a counselor, a doctor, or a finished story. I am building as I go. What I can offer is what I have learned, what Scripture actually says, and something practical you can do today. God met me while I was still trying to get up. That is where this book comes from.

Take what helps. Leave what does not. Get real help when you need it, because prayer sits beside treatment and safety, not instead of them.

You survived. Now we rebuild. — Nikki & Big Boy

How This Book Works§H3§

Every day has six pages, always in this order, so you never have to decide what to do next:

1
Guide · Understand and plan

Today’s goal, what the Bible passage actually says in its setting, what research suggests, and five numbered steps with check boxes.

2
Standing, left page

An optional grounding exercise, Scripture, and teaching on spiritual warfare, family wounds, and addiction.

3
Standing, right page

Reflection prompts, one soft action, a prayer, and a declaration.

4
Coming Home · Go to her

One gentle step toward the child you were, with a prayer, an affirmation, and a challenge.

5
Write it down

Rate your distress before and after, circle the steps you finished, and write what came up. Over time the numbers show you what actually helps.

6
Pocket page

A verse to carry, a note of love with an ESV verse, a nugget, “Today I choose,” and a note from Future Me.

Be honest about the science

  • The research notes are plain-language summaries of published studies. They describe what has been found across groups of people. They are not promises about you.
  • Citations were written from memory and have not been checked against the originals. Look up any you plan to rely on, and ask a counselor or doctor about anything that affects your care.
  • The Bible “in context” notes explain a passage’s setting. Where I apply a verse beyond its own subject, I say so.

Pace yourself

  • Do all six pages in one sitting, or spread them across the day. Doing only the Guide on a hard day still counts.
  • Skip any step or any grounding exercise that does not feel safe. Nothing here asks you to tell a story or remember anything.
  • This book does not replace counseling, treatment, medical care, or a safety plan. Prayer sits beside those things, not instead of them.

Going Back Safely§H6§

This book walks you through a prayerful, imaginative practice: visiting the child you were, comforting her, releasing what she promised to survive, and bringing her home to the woman you are becoming. It is a tool, not a cure, and these are the rules that keep it safe.

What it is

Prayerful imagination and compassion practice anchored in Scripture: God sees and comforts (Psalm 139:12; Isaiah 66:13), and Jesus welcomes children (Mark 10:14). The “room” and the “doorway” are pictures. They are not visions, and they are not literal memories.

What it is not

It is not memory recovery. You never hunt for memories, and you never try to reconstruct what you do not already know. It is not a ritual that frees anyone by itself, and it does not replace therapy, medicine, or safety planning. Imagining something does not make it true history.

Your rules

  • You choose the pace. A stop word, a ten-minute timer, and a landing (warm drink, walk, a text to someone) are part of every visit.
  • Visit from the doorway. You never have to go into a scene.
  • Use only what you already know. If nothing comes, nothing is required.
  • Jesus is central. If you cannot picture Him, pray His words aloud instead.
  • If you feel far away, numb, flooded, or have flashbacks, stop, open your eyes, find the date and the exit, and do your landing.

Do this with a trained trauma therapist if

  • your history includes severe or ongoing abuse, trafficking, or ritual abuse
  • you lose time, dissociate, or feel like parts of you are separate
  • visits leave you worse for more than a day

If you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988. If you are in danger, call 911.

Before day one

Spiritual Warfare, Plainly§H7§

I want to be careful with this language, because it has been used on people who needed help, not hype. So here is what I stand on.

What Scripture says

There is a real adversary: a liar, an accuser, a thief (John 10:10; Revelation 12:10; 1 Peter 5:8). He is a created being, limited by God (Job 1–2), and already defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15; 1 John 3:8). Our part is to submit to God, resist the devil, stand firm in the armor God gives, answer lies with what is written (as Jesus did in Matthew 4), and pray (James 4:7; Ephesians 6:10–18).

What Scripture does not say

It does not hand us a formula. In Acts 19:13–16, men tried to use Jesus’ name like a tool and were beaten. It does not say every problem is demonic. It does not say we should shout or boast about authority; Jesus told His disciples to rejoice not that spirits submit to them but that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20), and even the archangel Michael did not presume to rebuke the devil on his own (Jude 9). It does not say a child’s struggle is a spirit, or that words on a page break a curse.

How this book uses the word “warfare”

Here, warfare means refusing to agree with lies, standing in Christ, and doing the ordinary faithful things together with practical care: sleep, food, doctors, counselors, safety, honest friends, and prayer. Test every spirit (1 John 4:1). If something makes you more ashamed, more isolated, or more afraid, it is not from Him.

Where I offer a picture (doors, agreements, stages) it is interpretation. Scripture is the authority; the pictures are tools.

Before day one

A Word About Your Mother§H8§

This book was rewritten for you: a daughter whose mother carried her own trauma and addiction, and who allowed your father to abuse you when you were a baby; a woman in recovery from her own addiction; a woman who is not a mother and does not want to carry any of this on. If that is not your story, read it as the nearest true thing.

What I will not do

I will not ask you to remember. You were six months old; you cannot, and you do not need to. I will not tell you your mother was only a monster or only a victim; people are often both, and you can hold that without excusing her. I will not tell you your addiction is her fault, or that it is only yours. I will not tell you that you are destined to repeat it, or that you are cursed. I will not use guilt, and I will not tell you that forgiving means going back.

What I will do

Explain, plainly and without claiming certainty, how a baby who was not protected can grow into a woman whose body reaches for relief and whose heart struggles to trust (Days 5, 6, 39, 40). Name the grief for the mother you needed. Walk you through forgiving at your own pace, setting boundaries, and releasing what is not yours. Show you concrete ways to stop the pattern with you: recovery, therapy, safe people, new habits, and a line of faith and honesty you start now, with or without children.

Right now

If you are in danger, call 911. If you are thinking about ending your life, call or text 988. If a child is at risk near the person who harmed you, Childhelp: 1-800-422-4453. SAMHSA Helpline (substance use): 1-800-662-4357. (Please confirm numbers before relying on them.)

Say it before day one

An Opening Prayer§H9§

Say it again any day you need it.

Father, I come to You through Jesus. I am not coming cleaned up. I am coming honest.

You know what was done to me, what I did to get through it, and what I am still afraid is true about me. Nothing in these ninety days will surprise You.

Walk through each page with me. Where I find shame, bring light. Where I find grief, sit with me and do not rush me. Where I find anger, let me bring it to You instead of holding it against You.

Give me the courage to take the next small step, and the sense to ask for help when I need it. Let what I learn become something somebody else can use.

I put my sister Brandi Renee in Your hands, not mine. In Jesus’ name. Amen.

Arc 1 · Telling the TruthDay 01 / 90

The War Started Before You Had Words

Today’s goal

Name that the fight is real, and that you are not fighting it alone.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 6:12 (ESV)

Paul wrote Ephesians while under arrest in Rome, around AD 60–62, to believers in Ephesus. “Struggle” translates a wrestling word. He is not saying people are never responsible for what they do. He is saying there is more going on in the world than what we can see, and that we are told to stand, not to panic.

What research suggests

The large ACE study of more than 17,000 adults found that the more kinds of childhood adversity a person reported, the higher their risk of later problems, including substance use. It describes risk across a group. It does not say what will happen to you.

Source: Felitti et al., 1998. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Sit or stand where your feet can touch the floor. Set a timer for 2 minutes.
  2. Say out loud, “I am here. It is today. I am an adult.” Look around and name three things you can see.
  3. Read today’s verse once, slowly. Then read the “In context” box.
  4. Write on the Journal page the one sentence you most need to be true about this book.
  5. Say the declaration out loud. Check the box. Stop.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

What this means

You have told me that your father abused you when you were six months old, and that your mother, who carried her own trauma and addiction, allowed it. You had no words, no memory, and no defense. Scripture says the struggle is real and bigger than flesh and blood, and Jesus names the thief's work: to steal, kill, and destroy. What was done to you was never God's will. You are not crazy for living with effects you cannot explain, and you do not need a single memory to be believed here.

Arc 1 · Telling the TruthDay 02 / 90

Telling the Truth About Both of Them

Today’s goal

Tell the truth about both parents without lying in either direction.

The Bible in context · 1 John 1:7 (ESV)

First John was written by the apostle John to believers who were being taught confusing things about sin and about Jesus. Verse 7 says walking in the light brings fellowship and that Jesus’s blood cleanses us from all sin. Light in this letter means honesty before God, not performance.

What research suggests

In the classic 1986 study, people who wrote about a distressing event for a few days reported fewer health-center visits afterward than people who wrote about neutral topics. Later work found the average effect is modest and varies from person to person.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Get two sheets of paper. Head one “Mother” and one “Father.”
  2. For 5 minutes each, list what was true: what they did, what they failed to do, and what they did well. Use short phrases, not paragraphs.
  3. Put a star by anything you have never said to anyone. Do not explain it yet.
  4. Fold the pages and put them where no one will find them. You do not have to show anyone.
  5. Say the declaration. If you feel flooded, stop and do the 5-things-you-can-see reset.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.”1 John 1:7 · ESV
What this means

Families protect the ones who did the harm. Silence says the father's actions and the mother's failure to protect are not to be named. Light is not exposure for its own sake. It is one safe person who will not panic, gossip, or use it against you. Warfare begins small: saying out loud to one human being that your father hurt you and your mother did not protect you, and watching what the fear does when it is spoken.

Arc 1 · Telling the TruthDay 03 / 90

Both Hands: What Was Done and What You Did

Today’s goal

Hold what was done to you and what you did, without letting one erase the other.

The Bible in context · Romans 7:15 (ESV)

In Romans 7:15 Paul describes the struggle of doing what he does not want to do. He is writing to the church in Rome about the law, sin, and grace, and he is not hiding his own struggle. Chapter 8 follows with “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”

What research suggests

Researchers who study shame and guilt have found that shame (“I am bad”) tends to go with hiding and relapse risk, while guilt (“I did something wrong”) tends to go with repair. This is a pattern in groups of people, not a rule for you.

Source: Tangney & Dearing, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Draw a line down the middle of a page. Left: “What was done to me.” Right: “What I did.”
  2. Write three to five words in each column. No stories.
  3. Read the right-hand column aloud, then say, “I am accountable for this, and I am not disposable.”
  4. Read the left-hand column aloud, then say, “This was not my fault.”
  5. Say the declaration, then put a hand on your chest for five breaths.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.
7HE H0LY R3UP FOR ALLDay 3 · Guide
Arc 1 · Telling the TruthDay 03 / 90

Both Hands: What Was Done and What You Did

Mother Wound · Addiction
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 1.6 · 4.4 | Vol. II Ch. 10
Sanctuary · optionalName three things you can see and one thing you can hear. Father, meet me exactly where I am.
“For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.”Romans 7:15 · ESV
What this means

A baby has zero responsibility for what happens to her. None. And later, in your own addiction, some of what you did was your own doing, and some of it hurt people. Both are true at once. Holding only the first makes you a permanent victim. Holding only the second makes you your own warden. Your mother had both hands too: she was hurt, and she failed you. You can see that without excusing it. You need both hands to carry this, and God carries the rest.

The Accuser Says It Was Your Fault

Today’s goal

Spot the accuser’s voice and answer it with what Jesus has already said.

The Bible in context · Revelation 12:10 (ESV)

Revelation 12:10 is part of John’s vision, written to churches under pressure around the end of the first century. The “accuser of our brothers” is cast down, and verse 11 says believers conquered him “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony.” The accuser’s main work in Scripture is accusation, not creativity.

What research suggests

In a brain-imaging study, simply putting a name on an emotion (“angry,” “afraid”) was linked to less amygdala activity than other responses. Naming the feeling is a small, free tool, and it is not a cure.

Source: Lieberman et al., 2007. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write down the accusing sentence you hear most (for example, “It was your fault”). Use the exact words.
  2. Next to it write who is saying it: “My shame,” “My family,” “The accuser,” or “I don’t know.” Any answer is fine.
  3. Under it write one true sentence, such as “I was six months old,” or “I am forgiven.”
  4. Say the true sentence three times out loud, slowly.
  5. Say the declaration. Drink a glass of water.

Arc 1 · Telling the TruthDay 05 / 90

A Body That Learned Early

Today’s goal

Learn what your body learned, without needing the story.

The Bible in context · Psalm 56:8 (ESV)

Psalm 56 is attributed to David “when the Philistines seized him in Gath.” Verse 8 says, “You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?” God is described as someone who notices and keeps track of pain.

What research suggests

A review of slow-breathing studies found that breathing slowly (around six breaths a minute) is linked to measurable changes in heart-rate variability and to feeling calmer in many people. Trauma writers like Bessel van der Kolk describe how stress can be held in the body, though the science is still being refined.

Sources: Zaccaro et al., 2018; van der Kolk, 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Sit with your feet flat. Put one hand on your belly. Set a timer for 3 minutes.
  2. Breathe in through your nose for 4 counts. Let it out slowly for 6 counts. Repeat.
  3. Notice where your body is tight. Do not fix it. Just say, “There.”
  4. Say to your body, quietly: “Thank you for watching out for me. We can rest now.”
  5. If breathing makes you dizzy or anxious, stop and press your feet into the floor instead.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

“You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?”Psalm 56:8 · ESV
What this means

Your body learned things before you had words: that the world is not safe, that the people meant to protect you may not, that relief has to be found. Those lessons live in the nervous system, not in stories, which is why you can feel them without remembering anything. Fight, flight, freeze, and fawn were survival strategies, and a body that learned them that early may reach for relief quickly. That is not weak faith. It is a body doing a job it learned young. God keeps count of every tear.

Where the Baby Lives

Today’s goal

Give the very young part of you a place to be held, without going back into the fire.

The Bible in context · Isaiah 66:13 (ESV)

Isaiah 66:13 says, “As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you.” Isaiah is speaking to Jerusalem after exile. God is described with a mother’s tenderness, which does not mean your own mother did that for you. It means God offers it.

What research suggests

A review of human–animal interaction research reported that contact with a friendly animal is linked to lower stress and, in some studies, changes in oxytocin and cortisol. The findings are mixed and often small, but many people feel steadier with a companion nearby.

Source: Beetz et al., 2012. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Pick one soft thing: a blanket, a stuffed animal, or your dog’s warm back. Hold it for 2 minutes.
  2. Say softly, “I am here. I am the grown-up now.”
  3. Ask, “How old does the fear feel today?” Write only the number.
  4. Do not ask what happened. Just say hello to that age.
  5. Say the declaration and keep the soft thing close for the rest of the day.

Six Resets for an Old Alarm

Today’s goal

Learn one reset you can do anywhere in under two minutes.

The Bible in context · Psalm 46:10 (ESV)

Psalm 46:10 says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” The Hebrew word for “be still” can mean to relax your grip or let go. The psalm opens with God as “a very present help in trouble” and describes earthquakes, roaring waters, and nations in uproar, so “be still” is spoken in the middle of noise, not after it clears.

What research suggests

Slow breathing is linked in studies to calmer physiology. Separately, research on emotion regulation suggests that changing how we think about a situation early on (reappraisal) tends to work better than trying to push the feeling down once it is big.

Sources: Zaccaro et al., 2018; Gross, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Choose one reset to practice: (a) feet-on-floor, (b) 4-in/6-out breathing, (c) cold water on wrists, or (d) naming five things you see.
  2. Practice it now for 90 seconds while you are calm. Calm practice is how it works when you are not.
  3. Write on a card: “When it spikes, I will ______.” Put the card where you will see it.
  4. Tell one person which reset you chose.
  5. Say the declaration.

Inventory: Mother, Father, Me

Today’s goal

The Bible in context · Psalm 139:23-24 (ESV)

Psalm 139:23–24 reads, “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts! And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!” It is David’s prayer to be examined by someone who already knows him. He asks God to search, not to condemn.

What research suggests

Writing about hard experiences helps some people more when they also make plans for what to do next. Research on “if–then” plans found that people who wrote a specific plan (“If X happens, I will do Y”) were more likely to follow through than people who only intended to.

Sources: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986; Gollwitzer, 1999. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Medical Before Mystical

Today’s goal

Ask the practical questions: sleep, body, medication, safety, and professional help.

The Bible in context · Jeremiah 8:22 (ESV)

Jeremiah 8:22 asks, “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?” Gilead was known for healing balm. Jeremiah is grieving that help existed and the people were not being healed. The verse is not telling anyone to skip medicine. It is lamenting an unhealed wound.

What research suggests

A Cochrane review concluded that exercise is moderately more effective than no treatment for depression symptoms, although the quality of evidence varies. Exercise is not a replacement for therapy or medication when those are needed.

Source: Cooney et al., 2013. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write down when you last had a medical check-up, a dental visit, a blood test, or talked to a counselor.
  2. Circle one overdue thing. Write how you will start: “Call ______ on ______.”
  3. Write your top three sleep problems (falling asleep, staying asleep, nightmares). Underline one to bring up with a doctor.
  4. If you take medication, write one question you have about it. Do not stop or change it on your own.
  5. Say the declaration. Put the appointment in your phone before you close this book.

“Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?”Jeremiah 8:22 · ESV
What this means

Before you decide something is demonic, ask a doctor. Early trauma changes how the body handles stress, and addiction changes the brain, so sleep, mood, anxiety, and craving can feel like attack. Look for a therapist trained in trauma (approaches like EMDR or trauma-focused therapy are options), a doctor who understands addiction, and a recovery community. If you are physically dependent on alcohol, benzodiazepines, or barbiturates, withdrawal can be deadly; do not stop alone. Prayer and medicine are not enemies.

Arc 1 · Telling the TruthDay 10 / 90

A Date, and a Reason Bigger Than Fear

Today’s goal

Set a start date, a reason bigger than fear, and one person who knows.

The Bible in context · Proverbs 4:26 (ESV)

Proverbs 4:26 says, “Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure.” Proverbs is a collection of wisdom sayings, many of them written as a father instructing his child. Here the instruction is to pay attention to where you are walking, which is a call to be deliberate.

What research suggests

A study that tracked people forming a new daily habit found that it took anywhere from about 18 to 254 days to feel automatic, with a typical figure of about 66 days. Missing a single day did not ruin the process.

Source: Lally et al., 2010. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write today’s date at the top of a card. Write a start date for your daily practice time (same time, same place).
  2. Write your reason in one sentence. It has to be bigger than “because I should.”
  3. Choose one person to tell. Write their name.
  4. Send them a text: “I’m doing 90 days of something hard. Will you check on me on day 10, 30, and 60?”
  5. Say the declaration. Put the card on your mirror or fridge.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Addiction · Cycle-Breaking

“Ponder the path of your feet; then all your ways will be sure.”Proverbs 4:26 · ESV
What this means

Someday is a comfortable word. A date is a decision. If you are ready to stop using, pick the date, clear the first seventy-two hours, remove what needs removing, and tell three people. Add the reason: you do not want to carry on what was handed to you. That reason is bigger than fear, and it can hold you when a craving is loud. If medical detox is needed, do it first; call SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 11 / 90

What Your Mother Taught Without Words

Today’s goal

See one thing your home taught without words, and name what you would teach instead.

The Bible in context · John 8:32 (ESV)

In John 8:31–36 Jesus speaks to people who had believed in him: “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” In the very next lines he says that everyone who sins is a slave to sin and that “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.” Truth here is tied to Jesus himself and to staying with his word.

What research suggests

Attachment researchers have found that some adults who had difficult childhoods can describe them honestly and coherently and still have secure relationships in adulthood. The term is “earned security.” It suggests that the past shapes us without sealing our future.

Source: Roisman et al., 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the sentence: “In my house, nobody ever said it out loud, but the rule was ______.” Fill it in three different ways.
  2. Pick one. Write the opposite rule that you want for your life now.
  3. Say the new rule out loud once.
  4. Write one small action you did today that fits the new rule, even if it is tiny.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Mother Wound · Childhood
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 1.5 | Vol. II Ch. 12 (Stage 3)
Sanctuary · optionalName three things you can see and one thing you can hear. God, I am here. You are here. That is enough to start.
“...and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.”John 8:32 · ESV
What this means

Trauma does not only hurt. It teaches. Without a word, you may have learned that love comes with harm, that people who should protect you will not, that you are not worth protecting, and that relief is something you find on your own. Those lessons were installed when you were too small to argue. You may be living by house rules from a house that burned down. The work is not to hate the lessons but to notice them.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 12 / 90

Lie, Evidence, Truth: "I Wasn't Worth Protecting"

Today’s goal

Write one lie, the evidence against it, and the truth, in a three-line row.

The Bible in context · 2 Corinthians 10:4-5 (ESV)

In 2 Corinthians 10:3–5 Paul is defending his ministry to a church that had doubts about him. He says, “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds,” and speaks of taking every thought captive to obey Christ. The battle in this passage is over arguments and thoughts, not over bodies or people.

What research suggests

Cognitive therapy, which teaches people to check their thoughts against evidence, has been shown in clinical trials to help with depression and anxiety. Checking a thought is different from arguing with it, which usually feeds it.

Source: Gross, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the lie in the first line: “I wasn’t worth protecting.”
  2. Second line, “Evidence against this:” list two facts. For example, “I was an infant,” “Infants are not responsible for protecting themselves.”
  3. Third line, “What Scripture says:” write the verse reference from today’s page and put it in your own words.
  4. Read all three lines aloud in order.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

God is called the defender of the helpless. Do not give the Sunday School answer. Give the real one.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 13 / 90

The Names You Were Given

Today’s goal

Write down the names you were called, and hand them back.

The Bible in context · Isaiah 43:1 (ESV)

Isaiah 43:1 comes in the middle of God’s word to Israel after the Babylonian exile was announced: “But now thus says the LORD, he who created you… ‘Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.’” In Scripture, to be called by name means to be known and claimed. The promise was spoken to a people, and Christians read it as the character of the God who calls his own.

What research suggests

Self-compassion researchers have linked treating yourself kindly, remembering you are not alone in suffering, and noticing pain without exaggerating it to lower depression and anxiety. In one trial, an eight-week self-compassion program improved well-being compared with a waiting list.

Source: Neff, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write three names or labels you were called growing up. Write who said each one.
  2. Under each write: “That was their word, not mine.”
  3. Write one name God uses in Scripture for those who are his (child, beloved, redeemed, called).
  4. Say that name out loud, then say, “That is what I answer to.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

The Names You Were Given

Childhood · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 1.5 | Vol. II Ch. 12 (Stage 3), Ch. 48
Sanctuary · optionalLook around until your eyes find the exit. You can leave if you need to. Lord, You were here before I said anything.
“But now thus says the LORD, he who created you, O Jacob, he who formed you, O Israel: "Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine."”Isaiah 43:1 · ESV
What this means

Somebody named you and you answered. Damaged. The addict's daughter. Too much. Not enough. The one who is just like her. A name given in someone's worst moment can follow you for decades, and a family that cannot name its own harm often names the child instead. God gives names in love. Whatever you answer to will run your life, so it is worth asking who gave it to you and whether they had the right.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 14 / 90

Trading Names

Today’s goal

Choose a new name or phrase and practice answering to it.

The Bible in context · Revelation 2:17 (ESV)

Revelation 2:17 is part of Jesus’s message to the church in Pergamum: “To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.” The meaning of the white stone is debated by scholars. What is clear is the picture of being personally known and renamed by Jesus.

What research suggests

In a study on writing about life goals, people who wrote for a few days about their best possible future selves reported better well-being afterward than people who wrote about neutral topics. It is a small effect, and it works best when the writing is realistic.

Source: King, 2001. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write down three words you would want someone to use for you in five years (for example, steady, tender, brave).
  2. Pick one as your word for this week. Write it on a card.
  3. Say, “My word is ______. I am practicing it.” Out loud once.
  4. Write one small thing you did today that matches the word.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Trading Names

Warfare · Childhood
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 48 (Trading the Names) | Workbook 3.1
Sanctuary · optionalPress your palms together, then let go. Jesus, I do not have to perform for You.
“...To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it.”Revelation 2:17 · ESV
What this means

God renames people: Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel, Simon to Peter. His names point at who you are becoming. Trading names is not positive thinking. It is putting a new truth where the old one lived. Daughter of an addicted mother becomes daughter of God. Damaged goods becomes new creation. Addict becomes a woman in recovery. Cycle-breaker is a name you get to earn, a day at a time. Say the new one out loud each morning for thirty days.

It Was Not Your Fault. You Were Six Months Old.

Today’s goal

Say it to yourself in the words you would say to a baby: “It was not your fault.”

The Bible in context · Psalm 103:13 (ESV)

Psalm 103:13 says, “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him.” The psalm is attributed to David and praises God for forgiving, healing, and redeeming. It also says, “He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (v. 14). God knows how small and fragile we are.

What research suggests

Self-compassion studies suggest that speaking to yourself with the kindness you would give a friend is linked to lower self-criticism and less shame. It can feel odd and unearned at first, which is normal.

Source: Neff, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Find a photo of yourself as a baby or small child, or picture one. If you have none, write “baby me” on a card.
  2. Hold it for 30 seconds. Say, “It was not your fault.”
  3. Say it again slower. Notice your breath.
  4. If you feel overwhelmed, stop and press your feet on the floor.
  5. Say the declaration and finish with a glass of water.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 16 / 90

Why You Went Back

Today’s goal

Understand why you went back, without calling yourself stupid.

The Bible in context · Luke 22:31-32 (ESV)

In Luke 22:31–32 Jesus tells Peter at the Last Supper, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” Jesus says “when,” not “if,” and he knows Peter is about to fail. He prays for him ahead of time and gives him a future.

What research suggests

Researchers who study how people change describe it as a loop with relapses, not a straight line. Many people who eventually change a deep habit go through the cycle several times. It does not make the attempts worthless.

Source: Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the last time you went back (to a person, a place, a substance, a belief). Just the facts, in one sentence.
  2. Write what you were hoping to get. Common answers: comfort, belonging, numbness, being chosen.
  3. Write what it actually cost you.
  4. Write one need you could meet a different way this week.
  5. Say the declaration. Say, “I am turning again.”
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 17 / 90

Missing the Ones Who Hurt You

Today’s goal

Let yourself miss the people who hurt you, without going back to them.

The Bible in context · Psalm 107:9 (ESV)

Psalm 107 is a song of thanks for God’s rescue of people in different kinds of trouble: wanderers, prisoners, the sick, sailors in storms. Verse 9 says, “For he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things.” The refrain, “Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love,” returns after each rescue. Longing is treated as real and God as the one who meets it.

What research suggests

Putting a mixed feeling into words (“I miss him and I am angry at him”) is linked to lower emotional intensity in lab studies of affect labeling. Mixed feelings are normal after harm, and they do not mean you should return.

Source: Lieberman et al., 2007. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write two sentences: “I miss ______ because ______.” and “I do not miss ______ because ______.”
  2. Say both aloud. Notice that you can feel both without choosing one.
  3. Write one thing that satisfied you today that did not involve them (food, music, sunshine, a laugh).
  4. If the longing gets very loud, text a safe person: “I’m missing something I shouldn’t go back to.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Arc 2 · The Lies and the NamesDay 18 / 90

No Memory, No Problem

Today’s goal

Make peace with the gaps in your memory.

The Bible in context · Psalm 139:12 (ESV)

Psalm 139:12 says, “even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.” The whole psalm is David’s meditation on being known by God from before birth. The verse does not say you must remember. It says nothing is hidden from him.

What research suggests

Dan Siegel’s “window of tolerance” describes the zone where a person can feel and think at the same time. Many trauma-informed therapists work on widening that window in the present rather than pressing for memories. It is one model among several.

Source: Siegel, 1999. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “What I know for sure about my early life is ______.” Two or three lines.
  2. Write: “What I don’t know, and may never know, is ______.”
  3. Say, “I do not have to remember to heal.”
  4. Put a hand on your chest. Take five slow breaths.
  5. Say the declaration. Do not go looking for anything today.

What You Did While Surviving

Today’s goal

Name what you did to survive, without lying and without self-hatred.

The Bible in context · 1 Timothy 1:15 (ESV)

In 1 Timothy 1:15 Paul writes to Timothy in Ephesus, “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” Paul says this about a man who had persecuted the church. He names what he did and builds his life on grace anyway.

What research suggests

Studies of shame and guilt in people with substance problems have found that shame-prone people tend to do worse over time, while guilt (“I did something wrong, and I want to repair it”) is linked to better outcomes. How we name what we did matters.

Source: Tangney & Dearing, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. List three things you did to survive that you do not like. One line each.
  2. Next to each write what you were protecting yourself from.
  3. Mark each with “Own it” (needs repair) or “Understand it” (it was survival).
  4. For any “Own it,” write one small repair, such as an apology you can send or an amends you can plan.
  5. Say the declaration.

Living Amends, and Forgiving Yourself

Today’s goal

Plan one living amends and one act of self-forgiveness.

The Bible in context · Proverbs 28:13 (ESV)

Proverbs 28:13 says, “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.” It sits in a section the book itself says was copied by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). Notice the two verbs: confess and forsake. Mercy follows both.

What research suggests

A meta-analysis of forgiveness programs found that people who took part reported more forgiveness and less distress than people who did not. Forgiving someone is not the same as reconciling with them.

Source: Wade et al., 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

  2. Write one sentence of the amends: “I am sorry for ______. I will ______ from now on.”
  3. Write one thing you need to forgive yourself for. Say, “I release myself from carrying this alone.”
  4. Pick a day this week to act. Put it on the calendar.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 3 · The Realm and Your AuthorityDay 21 / 90

Two Realms, One Family

Today’s goal

Practice holding two realities: what you see, and what you cannot.

The Bible in context · 2 Corinthians 4:18 (ESV)

In 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 Paul writes that “we do not lose heart,” and that “as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” He is writing from deep affliction. The unseen realm is described as real and lasting, not as a place to hunt for threats.

What research suggests

Research on rumination suggests that repetitive worry about causes and meanings tends to deepen distress and does not solve the problem. A deliberate shift to a concrete action or to something you can see and touch is often more useful.

Source: Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “Things I can see and touch right now: ______.” Name five.
  2. Write: “Things I believe are true but cannot see: ______.” Name two or three, such as God’s presence, that I am forgiven, that this will end.
  3. Say, “Both are real. I will not chase the unseen to prove it.”
  4. Do one tangible, ordinary thing (wash a dish, fold a towel) as an act of faith in the visible world.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Warfare · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 2.1 | Vol. II Ch. 1, 11

“...as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.”2 Corinthians 4:18 · ESV
What this means

Spiritual warfare is not only for conferences. It meets us in a family where addiction, abuse, and silence ran for years: in what you believe about yourself, in cravings, in who you are drawn to. Scripture treats the unseen opposition as real and limited, and treats ordinary faithfulness as how we stand. You are not imagining what you lived through, and you do not have to make the fight dramatic. You have to show up, tell the truth, and keep Jesus near. People are not demons; the harm done through them was still wrong.

Four Categories at 2 a.m.

Today’s goal

Sort what scares you into four plain categories.

The Bible in context · 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (ESV)

First Thessalonians 5:21 says, “but test everything; hold fast what is good.” Paul is closing a letter to a young church in Thessalonica and has just said, “Do not despise prophecies” (v. 20). The instruction is to evaluate carefully, not to believe everything and not to dismiss everything.

What research suggests

Cognitive reappraisal, which means looking at a situation again and asking what else could explain it, has been associated with healthier emotion outcomes than suppressing the feeling. Sorting is a form of reappraisal.

Source: Gross, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the thing that scares you at night in one line.
  2. Check one: Is it (1) a body/medical thing, (2) a memory or trauma response, (3) a real-world danger, or (4) a spiritual concern I should pray and test?
  3. Match it to a next step: doctor, grounding and a counselor, a safety plan, or prayer and a trusted pastor.
  4. Write the next step and when you will do it.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

What He Cannot Do

Today’s goal

Say what the enemy cannot do, using only what Scripture says.

The Bible in context · 1 John 4:4 (ESV)

First John 4:4 says, “Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.” John is writing to believers about false teachers and about testing spirits (4:1). The “greater” is the Spirit of God in the believer. The verse is not about us being powerful. It is about him.

What research suggests

Albert Bandura’s work on self-efficacy suggests that people who believe they can handle a challenge, often because they have handled smaller ones, are more likely to try again after setbacks. Believing you can does not guarantee you will.

Source: Bandura, 1977. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “Three things I have already survived that I once thought I could not: ______.”
  2. Write the verse in your own words: “The One in me is greater than ______.”
  3. Say it standing up, out loud, once.
  4. Write one small hard thing you will do today to prove you can.
  5. Say the declaration.

Standing, Not Cowering

Today’s goal

Practice standing: feet down, breath slow, words true.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 6:13 (ESV)

Ephesians 6:13 says, “Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm.” The armor imagery likely echoes what Paul saw on the Roman soldiers guarding him. Notice the goal: stand firm. The armor is mostly defense, and every piece is something God provides.

What research suggests

Slow, controlled breathing is associated with a calmer heart rate and with a sense of steadiness in many studies, though results vary. It is a tool, not a cure.

Source: Zaccaro et al., 2018. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Stand with your feet hip-width. Press them into the floor.
  2. Breathe in for 4, out for 6, five times.
  3. Say out loud: “I stand on what is true. I do not have to run.”
  4. Name one thing in your day today that you are tempted to run from. Write what standing would look like.
  5. Say the declaration.

Submit, Then Resist

Today’s goal

Do the verse in order: submit first, then resist.

The Bible in context · James 4:7 (ESV)

James 4:7 says, “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” James wrote to scattered Jewish Christians, and this verse sits in a passage about pride, worldliness, and humility (4:1–10). Notice the order: submission to God comes first, and resistance rests on that, not on your own strength.

What research suggests

Making specific if–then plans (“If I feel the pull at 9 p.m., I will call my sponsor”) helps people carry out intentions more reliably than good intentions alone, according to a large body of work on implementation intentions.

Source: Gollwitzer, 1999. Full citations are in the back of the book.

  2. Write a submit sentence: “God, I give this to you: ______.” Say it as a prayer.

Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 2.5, 2.6 (Step 1) | Vol. II Step 8
Sanctuary · optionalFeel your feet on the floor. Keep your eyes open. Lord, You were here before I said anything.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”James 4:7 · ESV
What this means

The order matters. Submit to God first, then resist. For anyone in addiction, submission begins with an honest admission that you cannot do this on willpower, and that is not defeat; it is where help begins. Resisting without submitting is exhausting. Authority is not volume. Jesus answered temptation with a sentence of Scripture. Loud is for our own fear.

Arc 3 · The Realm and Your AuthorityDay 26 / 90

What Keeps Getting Fed: Anger at Both Parents

Today’s goal

Find what is feeding your anger and starve that part, not the person.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 4:26-27 (ESV)

Ephesians 4:26–27 says, “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.” Paul is quoting Psalm 4:4 and is not forbidding anger. He is warning about letting it sit and grow. Anger itself is treated as a signal, not as a sin.

What research suggests

Studies on rumination suggest that replaying anger in your head tends to keep it going rather than release it. Doing something physical, writing it out, or talking with someone safe may work better than rehearsing it.

Source: Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write what you are angry about. Use hard words if you need. No one will read this.
  2. Write what you would want to say to each person, in a letter you will not send.
  3. Walk fast for 5 minutes, or squeeze a towel, or do 20 pushes against a wall.
  4. Write one boundary you can set that protects you without punishing them.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

“Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil.”Ephesians 4:26-27 · ESV
What this means

Some struggles keep getting fed by the same things: unforgiveness, lies about yourself, anger left to rot, old vows, substances. Paul says anger is not the problem. Holding it past sundown gives the enemy room. Your anger at your father and your mother is not wrong; it is information that you were wronged. The work is to bring it to God and to safe people, so it does not spill on yourself, on your recovery, or on people who did not cause it.

Arc 3 · The Realm and Your AuthorityDay 27 / 90

Taken In

Today’s goal

Practice the thought that God takes you in when no one else did.

The Bible in context · Psalm 27:10 (ESV)

Psalm 27:10 says, “For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.” Psalm 27 is a psalm of David about trusting God in danger. The line acknowledges real abandonment and says God receives the one who was abandoned. It does not say that the abandonment was fine.

What research suggests

A large meta-analysis found that people with stronger social relationships had a lower risk of early death than people with weaker ones. Belonging seems to matter for health, and God’s taking you in is not the only kind of belonging he provides.

Source: Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Read the verse aloud three times, slower each time.
  2. Write the two names of people who have been safe for you, even briefly. Add one place, one animal, or one community.
  3. Write: “God, take me in. Here is where I feel unsheltered: ______.”
  4. Plan one contact with a safe person this week and put it on the calendar.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

“For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.”Psalm 27:10 · ESV
What this means

Before anything else, get under cover. David knew what it was to be left: his father and mother had forsaken him, and the Lord took him in. You do not have to pretend your parents were safe in order to receive a safe God. Say who you belong to. Say what you cannot do alone. This is not a spell, and it does not guarantee a trouble-free life. It is a child running to the one who is bigger, and being taken in.

Forgiving a Mother Who Did Not Protect You

Today’s goal

Start the long, honest work of forgiving without pretending it is done.

The Bible in context · Colossians 3:13 (ESV)

Colossians 3:13 says, “bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.” Paul is writing to a church about clothing themselves in compassion. Forgiveness here is rooted in what Jesus has done, and it does not erase the “complaint.” The wrong is real.

What research suggests

In a meta-analysis of forgiveness interventions, people who were helped to forgive reported better outcomes, but the best results came in programs that took time and addressed the emotional experience, not just the decision.

Source: Wade et al., 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the name of the person you are working toward forgiving.
  2. Write what you are still angry about. Do not skip it.
  3. Write: “I am willing to be willing to forgive. I am not there yet, and that is okay.”
  4. Pray: “Jesus, you forgave from the cross. Help me with this one, one inch at a time.”
  5. Say the declaration. Do not contact the person unless it is safe and wise.
My notes while I do these steps

Forgiving a Mother Who Did Not Protect You

Mother Wound · Warfare
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 2.6 (Step 3) | Vol. II Step 10
Sanctuary · optionalPut a hand on your chest and let one long breath out. Holy Spirit, stay near, and do not let me go further than I can hold.
“bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.”Colossians 3:13 · ESV
What this means

Forgiveness is not saying it was okay and not reconciliation. It is releasing the right to collect. A mother who did not protect you, perhaps because of her own trauma and addiction, still did not protect you. Both are true: she may have been hurt and she hurt you. Forgive in pieces if you have to, out loud, one thing at a time, and let God keep the ledger. If she is gone, forgiveness can happen without her. You can forgive fully and keep every boundary.

Forgiven Is Not Back In

Today’s goal

Write what forgiven-but-not-back-in looks like for you.

The Bible in context · Proverbs 22:3 (ESV)

Proverbs 22:3 says, “The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.” Proverbs treats wisdom as seeing a real danger and acting. It is not unloving to stay out of a place that has hurt you.

What research suggests

People with several adverse childhood experiences are at higher average risk for later problems, which is why safe relationships and stable environments matter so much in recovery. This supports staying away from places and people that repeat the harm.

Source: Felitti et al., 1998. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “I forgive ______ and I will not ______.” Fill in the blank with a real boundary.
  2. Write three warning signs that you are being pulled back in.
  3. Write what you will do when you see them (leave, call someone, close the app, drive away).
  4. Share your boundary with one safe person.
  5. Say the declaration.

Forgiven Is Not Back In

Mother Wound · Warfare
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 7.2 | Vol. II Step 25
Sanctuary · optionalLook around until your eyes find the exit. You can leave if you need to. God, I am here. You are here. That is enough to start.
“The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.”Proverbs 22:3 · ESV
What this means

Forgiveness is between you and God. Reconciliation requires two people and real repentance. Where someone has harmed you or could harm you, safety decides access, not guilt or family pressure. Jesus withdrew often, and Paul named people and told others to avoid them. If your mother or father reaches out, you have options: no contact, limited contact, contact with conditions. This is not unforgiveness. It is wisdom, and in recovery it may be survival.

Armor for the Daughter Who Wasn't Protected

Today’s goal

Put on the armor, one piece at a time, with your hands.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 6:14-15 (ESV)

Ephesians 6:14–15 says, “Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and, as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace.” Verses 16–17 add the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Paul is describing what God provides, and in verse 18 he adds prayer.

What research suggests

Habit research suggests that actions repeated in the same place and time become automatic partly because the setting itself becomes a cue. Pairing the armor practice with a regular cue, like brushing your teeth, can make it easier to keep.

Source: Wood & Neal, 2007. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Stand up. Touch your waist and say, “Truth.” Touch your chest and say, “Righteousness, the right standing Jesus gave me.” Touch your feet and say, “Peace.”
  2. Raise one arm as if holding a shield. Say, “Faith.” Touch your head and say, “Salvation.” Open your hand and say, “The word.”
  3. Say a one-sentence prayer: “Lord, I put on what you provide.”
  4. Pick a cue (brushing your teeth, starting the car) to repeat this each morning.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 4 · The ContractsDay 31 / 90

Conclusions Drawn Before You Could Speak

Today’s goal

Find one agreement you made as a child and read it as a child’s conclusion.

The Bible in context · Colossians 2:14 (ESV)

Colossians 2:14 speaks of God “by cancelling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.” Paul is writing to a church being pressured by rules and spiritual experiences, and he says Christ has dealt with the list of charges. For Christians this is the basis for believing that the “paperwork” against you is not the last word.

What research suggests

Writing about an experience several days in a row is associated, on average, with modest improvements in well-being, partly because people begin to organize what happened into a story. It does not work equally well for everyone, and it is not a substitute for treatment.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Finish this sentence three ways: “When I was little, I decided that ______.”
  2. Circle the one that has run your life the most.
  3. Write how old you were when you decided it. A guess is fine.
  4. Say, “That was a child’s conclusion. It was reasonable then. I can revisit it now.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Conclusions Drawn Before You Could Speak

Warfare · Childhood
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 2.4 | Vol. II Ch. 1, 2
Sanctuary · optionalSit with your back against something solid. Lord, You were here before I said anything.
“by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.”Colossians 2:14 · ESV
What this means

Scripture uses the language of debts and records, and Colossians 2:14 says Christ canceled the record that stood against us. This book uses a courtroom picture for the beliefs, vows, and conclusions people live by without choosing them. A baby does not make vows, but a body draws conclusions: I am not safe, no one comes, I have to take care of myself. Those can run an adult life. Christians hold different views on how literally to take the picture. What is clear is that Jesus came to set captives free, and you may look honestly at what you have been living by.

Arc 4 · The ContractsDay 32 / 90

The Survival Vow: "I'll Never Need Anyone"

Today’s goal

Hear the vow plainly: “I will never need anyone.”

The Bible in context · Matthew 5:37 (ESV)

In Matthew 5:37 Jesus says, “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything more than this comes from evil.” He is teaching in the Sermon on the Mount about oaths, and says people should not need to swear to be believed. The point is honest, simple speech. Vows made out of fear and pain are not treated here as binding on you in Jesus’s name.

What research suggests

Attachment research suggests that people who learned early not to rely on others can learn to depend on safe people later, often through repeated experiences with someone steady. It takes time and it is not about willpower.

Source: Roisman et al., 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the vow you made in your own words: “I will never ______.”
  2. Write what it protected you from.
  3. Write what it has cost you: friendships, love, help, rest.
  4. Say it out loud once: “I made this vow to survive. I understand why.”
  5. Say the declaration. Do not try to release it today. Just look at it.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

The Survival Vow: "I'll Never Need Anyone"

Childhood · Cycle-Breaking
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 2.4 | Vol. II Ch. 3 (Contract 1), Ch. 4
Sanctuary · optionalTake a slow sip of water. Jesus, I do not have to perform for You.
“Let what you say be simply 'Yes' or 'No'; anything more than this comes from evil.”Matthew 5:37 · ESV
What this means

Somewhere in childhood most survivors make a rule to stay alive. I will never need anyone. I will never cry. I will never be like her. It worked then, and it may be running your adult life, including the reason you cannot let anyone hold you. Even a vow made to be the opposite of someone binds you to her, because you are still living in reaction. Jesus told us to stop swearing oaths. Not because He is harsh, but because He knows vows made in fear are heavy.

Arc 4 · The ContractsDay 33 / 90

Releasing a Child's Promise

Today’s goal

Release a child’s promise in prayer, in your own words.

The Bible in context · Mark 10:14 (ESV)

In Mark 10:13–14 people were bringing children to Jesus and the disciples scolded them. Jesus was indignant and said, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.” The scene shows Jesus welcoming the young and the powerless, and removing the obstacles people put in front of them.

What research suggests

Compassion-focused approaches suggest that people who speak to their younger or hurting selves with kindness often feel less shame over time. The effects are modest on average and vary a lot from person to person.

Source: Neff, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Read yesterday’s vow aloud.
  2. Write a prayer: “Jesus, she made this promise to survive. I am letting her put it down. Hold it for her.”
  3. Pray it aloud or whisper it.
  4. Write what you will do differently in one small way this week (ask for help, accept an offer, say no to something).
  5. Say the declaration. Do something kind for the child in you, such as a favorite snack or a nap.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Releasing a Child's Promise

Childhood · Warfare
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 4 (inner-vow work) | Workbook 2.6 (Step 5)
Sanctuary · optionalFeel your feet on the floor. Keep your eyes open. Father, meet me exactly where I am.
“...Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.”Mark 10:14 · ESV
What this means

Jesus welcomed children and did not make them earn it. When you find the vow, speak to the child who made it, not to scold her but to release her. Say: I see you. You made that promise because you had to, and it worked. I am the adult now, and you do not have to hold the door anymore. Then, in Jesus' name, release the vow and replace it with something true: I can let safe people in. I can feel and still be okay. I can want things. A woman who learns this breaks a chain that ran before her.

Words Over You, and Words You Say to Yourself

Today’s goal

Replace one thing you say to yourself with something true and kind.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 4:29 (ESV)

Ephesians 4:29 says, “Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.” It is addressed to a church about how they speak to each other. It also fits how we speak to ourselves, though that is an application, not the verse’s direct subject.

What research suggests

In studies of self-talk, people who addressed themselves by name or as “you” (instead of “I”) while stressed often reported less anxiety and performed better under pressure. It is a simple tool, and results differ among people.

Source: Kross et al., 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the mean thing you say to yourself most. Exact words.
  2. Cross it out with one line.
  3. Write what you would say to a friend in the same situation.
  4. Say it to yourself using your name: “______, you are doing the best you can with what you have.”
  5. Say the declaration.

Words Over You, and Words You Say to Yourself

Mother Wound · Cycle-Breaking
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 6 | Workbook 2.6 (Step 5)
Sanctuary · optionalHold something warm or cold in your hands for a minute. Holy Spirit, stay near, and do not let me go further than I can hold.
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear.”Ephesians 4:29 · ESV
What this means

Words matter. Many of us can still hear what was said over us: you will never amount to anything, you are just like your mother. We also repeat those words to ourselves, and sometimes to others in our worst hour. You cannot unsay what was said to you, but you can say something truer, and you can stop passing it on. Say it plainly. Repair what you can. Words can wound, and words can bless.

Arc 4 · The ContractsDay 35 / 90

The Shame Covenant: Being Her Daughter

Today’s goal

Notice the shame that belongs to somebody else and hand it back.

The Bible in context · Psalm 34:5 (ESV)

Psalm 34:5 says, “Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed.” The psalm is attributed to David after he escaped from Abimelech (Achish) by pretending to be insane. The shame in view is the disgrace of being abandoned, and the answer is looking to God.

What research suggests

Research on shame and addiction suggests that shame often drives hiding, and hiding often drives relapse. People who tend toward guilt (“I did something wrong”) over shame (“I am wrong”) tend to take more steps to repair.

Source: Tangney & Dearing, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one thing you are ashamed of that someone else did to you or put on you.
  2. Write: “This is not mine. I am handing it back.”
  3. Take a piece of paper, write the shame on it, and tear it in four pieces. Throw it away.
  4. Say a short prayer: “Jesus, take it. I do not need it.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

The Shame Covenant: Being Her Daughter

Mother Wound · Warfare
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 3 (Contract 14) | Workbook 1.6
Sanctuary · optionalName three things you can see and one thing you can hear. God, I am here. You are here. That is enough to start.
“Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed.”Psalm 34:5 · ESV
What this means

Shame is not the same as guilt. Guilt says I did something wrong. Shame says I am something wrong. A child of an addicted, absent, or complicit parent often carries shame that is not hers: the family's reputation, the secrets, the smell of the house. Shame hides, and the hiding feeds it. Safe light is what shame cannot stand. That means looking toward Him, not at your reflection in other people's faces.

Arc 4 · The ContractsDay 36 / 90

The Silence Contract: Family Secrets

Today’s goal

Break one silence in a safe way.

The Bible in context · Psalm 32:3 (ESV)

Psalm 32:3 says, “For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.” David is describing what concealing sin did to him, and verse 5 continues, “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.” The relief came when he spoke. This is about confession to God, which can include a safe person.

What research suggests

Studies of expressive writing suggest that putting secrets into words can reduce the load they carry, even when no one reads them. When possible, telling a safe, trained person can help more than writing alone.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one secret in a sentence. No details needed.
  2. Decide who is safe: a counselor, a pastor you trust, a recovery sponsor, a close friend, or God alone for now.

Today’s goal

The Bible in context · 1 Corinthians 6:17 (ESV)

First Corinthians 6:17 says, “But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.” Paul is writing to the church at Corinth about sexual immorality and about bodies belonging to the Lord. The ties we form to people and substances are real emotionally and in the body. The Bible’s answer is a stronger union with Christ, not a ritual.

What research suggests

Attachment research shows that early bonds shape how we connect later, including to people who are not good for us. Trauma-informed therapists often describe this as a pattern that can be understood and gradually changed.

Source: Roisman et al., 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Releasing the Hold

Today’s goal

Practice releasing: give back what was never yours to carry.

The Bible in context · Philippians 3:13-14 (ESV)

Philippians 3:13–14 says, “Brothers, I do not consider that I have made it my own. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.” Paul wrote from prison and in the same letter says he has not yet arrived. Forgetting here means not letting the past define the race, not erasing it.

What research suggests

Research on habits suggests that changing cues in your environment can make it easier to break old patterns. Removing reminders, changing routes, and changing routines help more than relying on willpower alone.

Source: Wood & Neal, 2007. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one object, number, place, or app connected to what pulls you back.
  2. Decide: delete, hide, move, or give away. Do it now, or put a time on it.
  3. Write one new cue to replace it (a photo, a verse card, a different route).
  4. Say, “I am pressing on.”
  5. Say the declaration.

What this means

You can release your hold on a person and ask God to loosen their hold on you. Hand back what is theirs: the shame, the blame, the voice in your head, their version of you. Where contact is ongoing, the release is internal and the practical is separate: boundaries, limited contact, someone who can help you hold them. Pressing forward is not pretending. It is a direction.

The Cistern: What the Substance Gave You That She Didn't

Today’s goal

Find what you were really thirsty for.

The Bible in context · Jeremiah 2:13 (ESV)

Jeremiah 2:13 says, “for my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.” God, speaking through Jeremiah, describes his people trying to meet a real need in places that cannot hold it. It names the thirst as legitimate and the cistern as the problem.

What research suggests

Behavioral activation, a well-studied approach, helps people re-engage with activities that give a sense of meaning and pleasure instead of avoiding or numbing. In one trial it did as well as other treatments for depression. It works by doing, not by waiting to feel like it.

Source: Dimidjian et al., 2006. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write what the substance or pattern gave you: relief, belonging, energy, quiet, feeling chosen.
  2. Next to each, write one healthier source of it.
  3. Pick one activity from that list and schedule it for a specific time today or tomorrow.
  4. Do it, even for ten minutes. Note afterward how you feel.
  5. Say the declaration.

The Bond You Mistook for Love

Today’s goal

Learn the difference between a trauma bond and love.

The Bible in context · 1 John 4:18 (ESV)

First John 4:18 says, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.” John is writing about God’s love and about how believers love each other. Love here is described as safe, not as a source of terror.

What research suggests

Studies of adverse childhood experiences show that early harm can make unsafe relationships feel familiar. Many people feel strongest pulled toward patterns that echo childhood, even when the patterns hurt them.

Control and the Fear of Becoming Her

Today’s goal

The Bible in context · Matthew 6:27 (ESV)

In Matthew 6:27 Jesus asks, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” It is part of the Sermon on the Mount, in a stretch about not being anxious about food, clothes, or tomorrow. He points to birds and flowers, and he is not telling people to be careless. He is telling them they are not in charge of everything.

What research suggests

Studies of rumination suggest that trying to think your way to total certainty usually increases worry. Acting on one small thing and then letting go tends to help more.

Source: Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Worth That Isn't Work or Rescue

Today’s goal

Receive worth that is not earned by work or rescue.

The Bible in context · Luke 10:41-42 (ESV)

In Luke 10:38–42 Jesus visits Martha and Mary. Martha is “distracted with much serving” and asks him to tell Mary to help. Jesus answers, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.” He is not shaming work. He is pointing out that Martha is being pulled apart by it.

What research suggests

Self-compassion research has linked treating yourself kindly with greater motivation and resilience, not laziness. People who are kind to themselves after a failure are often more likely to try again.

Source: Neff, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the ways you try to earn love (fix, give, please, perform).
  2. Write how you feel when you stop doing them.
  3. Choose a 15-minute period today to simply sit and do nothing useful. Sit.
  4. Say, “I am loved at rest.”
  5. Say the declaration.
