Self-Punishment: Paying for Her Sins and Yours

Today’s goal

Stop punishing yourself for what the Lord has already carried.

The Bible in context · Romans 8:1 (ESV)

Romans 8:1 says, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” It comes after Romans 7, where Paul describes struggling with sin. “Therefore” ties it to the argument: the verdict has already been handled in Christ. Conviction that moves you toward repair can come from God. Condemnation that keeps you in the dock does not.

What research suggests

Research suggests that harsh self-punishment tends to increase hiding, not repair. Repair after a mistake is more likely when people feel responsible but not worthless.

Source: Tangney & Dearing, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one way you punish yourself (starving, isolating, overworking, using, harming).
  2. Write what you think it pays for.
  3. Write: “Jesus already paid for this. I do not need to.”
  4. Replace the punishment with one kind, concrete act (a meal, a shower, a nap, a call).
  5. If the urge to hurt yourself is strong, call or text 988 or tell a safe person now. Say the declaration.

Arc 4 · The ContractsDay 44 / 90

Wanting Out

Today’s goal

Get through a dark day safely.

The Bible in context · 1 Kings 19:4-5 (ESV)

In 1 Kings 19:4–5 Elijah, exhausted and afraid after Jezebel’s threat, goes a day’s journey into the wilderness and asks that he might die: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life.” God does not scold him. An angel touches him and says, “Arise and eat.” Rest and food come first. The fuller conversation with God comes later.

What research suggests

If you are thinking about ending your life, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline offers free, confidential support by call or text, any hour, in the U.S. Wanting to disappear is a sign of overwhelming pain, not a character flaw, and it can be spoken about out loud.

Source: 988 Lifeline (988lifeline.org).

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. If you are in danger right now, call or text 988 (or call 911). Stay with someone if you can.
  2. Tell one safe person in plain words: “I am having a dark day. Can you stay on the phone with me?”
  3. Eat or drink something. Elijah’s first step was food and sleep.
  4. Remove anything you could use to hurt yourself from reach, or ask someone to hold it for you.
  5. Say the declaration. Do one tiny thing today and tell someone how it went.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Wanting Out

Warfare · Addiction
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 3 (Contract 18) | Workbook Resources
Sanctuary · optionalPut a hand on your chest and let one long breath out. Jesus, I do not have to perform for You.
“But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers." And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat."”1 Kings 19:4-5 · ESV
What this means

A death wish is a symptom, not a sin, and not a truth. Elijah, Jonah, Job, and Moses all asked to die, and God's answer to Elijah was food, sleep, a whisper, and a new job, not a rebuke. Early trauma and addiction both raise the risk of wanting out. If that thought has teeth today, call or text 988 (or call 911) before you read another word. You can also tell your sponsor, a counselor, or a friend. This is not weakness; it is the correct use of help.

The Accuser's Pen: "You're Just Like Her"

Today’s goal

Take back the pen from the accuser’s “You’re just like her.”

The Bible in context · Zechariah 3:1-4 (v. 2 quoted) (ESV)

In Zechariah 3:1–4 the prophet sees Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, with Satan at his right hand to accuse him. The LORD says, “The LORD rebuke you, O Satan!” and asks, “Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?” Joshua’s filthy garments are removed, and he is told, “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments.” The accuser speaks, God answers, and the clothing is changed.

What research suggests

Self-talk research suggests that how we address ourselves, with distance and kindness, can reduce the sting of harsh self-evaluation. A small shift in wording can change how a thought lands.

Source: Kross et al., 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the accusation: “You’re just like her.”
  2. Write what is the same about you and her and what is different. Be honest and specific.
  3. Write three choices you made this year that she did not make or could not make.
  4. Rewrite the pen line: “I am not her. I am my own woman, and I am choosing differently.”
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 5 · The BloodlineDay 46 / 90

Terrain, Not Guilt: What You Inherited

Today’s goal

Separate what you inherited from what you are guilty of.

The Bible in context · Ezekiel 18:20 (ESV)

Ezekiel 18:20 says, “The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.” Ezekiel was speaking to Judean exiles in Babylon who were saying, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.” God answers that each person is accountable for their own sin. You may inherit terrain, but not guilt.

What research suggests

Twin and family studies suggest that genetics account for a meaningful share (often estimated around 40–60 percent) of vulnerability to addiction, and adverse childhood experiences add risk. Both describe risk, not destiny, and neither is moral guilt.

Sources: Goldman et al., 2005; Felitti et al., 1998. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Make two columns: “What I may have inherited (terrain)” and “What I am responsible for now (choices).”
  2. Under terrain, list things like family history of addiction, early stress, learned coping.
  3. Under choices, list things you can do: treatment, meetings, boundaries, sleep, supports.
  4. Say: “I did not choose the terrain. I do choose the path.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Terrain, Not Guilt: What You Inherited

Mother Wound · Cycle-Breaking
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 6.1 | Vol. II Ch. 8
Sanctuary · optionalPress your palms together, then let go. Holy Spirit, stay near, and do not let me go further than I can hold.
“The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself.”Ezekiel 18:20 · ESV
What this means

Guilt does not transfer. You are not guilty of your mother's addiction or your father's abuse. But terrain does: patterns, wounds, habits, biology, silence. Research suggests addiction runs in families through both genes and environment, and scientists are still learning how. Exodus 20:5 says consequences reach down generations; Ezekiel 18 says each person answers for their own; the same Bible says God's steadfast love reaches thousands. You did not inherit their sin. You inherited the ground it grew on, and you get to change what grows.

Drawing the Family Line

Today’s goal

Find one good thing in your family line and honor it.

The Bible in context · Psalm 78:4 (ESV)

Psalm 78:4 says, “We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done.” Psalm 78 is a long historical psalm attributed to Asaph that tells Israel’s story, including their failures, so that the next generation will not repeat them and will trust God. Passing on truth, good and hard, is the point.

What research suggests

In a series of studies, people asked to list things they were grateful for each week reported greater well-being than those who listed hassles. Gratitude does not erase pain, but it can balance what we notice.

Source: Emmons & McCullough, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Four Layers: How It Passed to You, and How It Stops

Today’s goal

Map the four layers: body, home, learning, and spirit, and how each can change.

The Bible in context · Romans 12:2 (ESV)

Romans 12:2 says, “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.” Paul writes this after eleven chapters of explaining what God has done. Transformation is described as ongoing and as happening by renewal, which fits how habits are changed.

What research suggests

Addiction risk is shaped by biology, environment, and learning, and each of those layers can be addressed. Bandura’s work suggests that behaviors we learn from watching others can be replaced by new ones we see modeled and practice.

Sources: Goldman et al., 2005; Bandura, 1977. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Draw four boxes: Body, Home, Learning, Spirit.
  2. In each, write one way it affected you, and one change you can make (Body: sleep and treatment; Home: who you live with; Learning: new habits; Spirit: prayer and community).
  3. Choose one change to start this week.
  4. Write the first step and the date.
  5. Say the declaration.

Four Layers: How It Passed to You, and How It Stops

Cycle-Breaking · Warfare
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 6.1 | Vol. II Ch. 8

“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.”Romans 12:2 · ESV
What this means

A pattern can travel four ways. Behavioral: you learn what you saw. Biological: severe stress can shape how bodies respond, and addiction risk runs in families. Systemic: poverty, instability, and lack of support are real walls. Spiritual: Scripture speaks of the enemy and of unhealed wounds, and Christians differ on how to understand this layer. Most people fight one layer and wonder why it did not hold. Work all four: practice new behavior, protect sleep and health, build support, and bring it to God.

Where It May Have Started

Today’s goal

Remember that you did not start it.

The Bible in context · Lamentations 5:7 (ESV)

Lamentations 5:7 says, “Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities.” Lamentations is a collection of laments over the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. This verse is the cry of people feeling the weight of what came before. Notice that it is a lament, not a doctrine. It describes pain and does not command anyone to accept it forever.

What research suggests

Early research on abuse found that a minority (often cited around one-third) of abused children went on to abuse their own children, which means most did not. The finding is old and debated, but it supports the point that the pattern can be broken.

Source: Kaufman & Zigler, 1987. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “It started before me. The first person in my family I know of who ______ was ______.” If you do not know, write “I do not know.”
  2. Write: “I am not the beginning of this.”
  3. Write: “I can be the end of it.”
  4. Pray: “Lord, I name what I have inherited. I am asking you to meet me here.”
  5. Say the declaration.

“Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities.”Lamentations 5:7 · ESV

For each pattern, ask where it may have started. What was done to your mother? What was done to your grandmother? What did your family lose, flee, or hide? You will not always find an answer, and you are not required to. Understanding your mother's story is not excusing it, and it does not mean you owe her anything. It may help you see that the harm did not start with you, and that some of what looked like cruelty was another wounded person's survival. Hold it with humility.

Standing in the Gap for a Family That Didn't Stand for You

Today’s goal

Stand in the gap in prayer, without taking on the family’s sin as your debt.

The Bible in context · Nehemiah 1:6 (ESV)

In Nehemiah 1:6 Nehemiah prays, “let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father’s house have sinned.” He was cupbearer to the Persian king, hearing that Jerusalem’s walls were broken. He prays honestly, includes himself, and then acts.

What research suggests

A review of studies on Alcoholics Anonymous and similar programs found that they were as effective as or more effective than other treatments at helping people stay abstinent, and they cost less. Community matters in recovery.

Source: Kelly et al., 2020. Full citations are in the back of the book.

  2. Write one honest line about yourself: “I too have ______.”

  4. Do the action today or schedule it.
  5. Say the declaration.

Cycle-Breaking · Warfare

“let your ear be attentive and your eyes open, to hear the prayer of your servant that I now pray before you day and night for the people of Israel your servants, confessing the sins of the people of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Even I and my father's house have sinned.”Nehemiah 1:6 · ESV
What this means

Nehemiah prayed for his people with the words we have sinned, including himself. Daniel did too. Many believers find this meaningful for family patterns: you do not take on their guilt, you agree with God about what is true, and you ask for mercy on your line. It is a practice to consider, not a requirement for freedom or a magic formula. If it does not sit right, skip it and talk to a pastor you trust. It may feel strange to pray for those who failed you; you can do it without defending them.

A Prayer for the Line, Including Whoever Comes After You

Today’s goal

Write a prayer for those who came before and those who come after.

The Bible in context · Exodus 34:6 (ESV)

Exodus 34:6 says, “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.” In the next verses God also says he visits the iniquity of fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation. Read together, verse 6 is the lead: his character is mercy. The generational line is a real consequence of sin spreading, while his steadfast love extends to thousands.

What research suggests

Writing about your best possible future, as in studies of life-goal writing, has been linked to better well-being. It tends to help most when you also say what you will do.

Source: King, 2001. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box

  2. Write a prayer for yourself.
  3. Write a prayer for anyone who comes after you (nieces, nephews, friends’ children, people you will mentor).
  4. Read all three aloud.
  5. Say the declaration.

Agreements We Repeat: "We're All Addicts"

Today’s goal

Replace one family saying with a true one.

The Bible in context · Proverbs 26:2 (ESV)

Proverbs 26:2 says, “Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight.” Proverbs uses vivid images from nature. The verse says an undeserved curse does not land. Words spoken over you that have no cause do not have the power they claimed.

What research suggests

Research on self-talk suggests that how you speak to yourself, even something as small as using your name, can change how a stress response feels. Replacing a familiar phrase with a new one takes repetition.

Source: Kross et al., 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the saying you heard growing up (for example, “We’re all addicts,” “Nothing ever works out for us”).
  2. Write who said it and what they were afraid of.
  3. Write a true replacement: “Some of us struggled. I am choosing recovery.”
  4. Say the replacement ten times today when you notice the old one.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 5 · The BloodlineDay 53 / 90

New Behavior, Practiced Badly: Learning What Was Never Modeled

Today’s goal

Practice one thing nobody taught you, as a beginner.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 4:23-24 (ESV)

Ephesians 4:23–24 says, “and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.” Paul talks about taking off the old self and putting on the new, like changing clothes. It is something you practice, not something you feel your way into.

What research suggests

Bandura’s research on learning suggests that people learn by watching others and by practicing in small steps, and that early successes increase confidence. Being a beginner is a normal part of learning.

Source: Bandura, 1977. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Choose one skill nobody taught you (asking for help, saying no, budgeting, apologizing, resting).
  2. Watch or read about it for ten minutes (a safe person, a short video, a book).
  3. Practice it once today in a small way.
  4. Write what happened and how it felt.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 5 · The BloodlineDay 54 / 90

Honor Without Repeating

Today’s goal

Honor without repeating.

The Bible in context · Exodus 20:12 (ESV)

Exodus 20:12 says, “Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.” It is the fifth of the Ten Commandments. In the Bible, honor is not blind obedience to harm, and elsewhere in Scripture God warns against abuse and calls parents to care for their children. Honor can mean treating someone with basic dignity, telling the truth about them, and keeping your distance when needed.

What research suggests

Attachment research suggests that people with painful childhoods can build secure relationships over time, even if they keep boundaries with their families. Distance and dignity are not opposites.

Source: Roisman et al., 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one way you can honor your parent(s) without getting hurt (pray for them, speak kindly of the good, keep the peace from a distance).
  2. Write one thing that would not be honor (taking blame, enabling, lying).
  3. Write one boundary you will keep.
  4. Say, “I can honor the person without repeating the pattern.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps

“Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.”Exodus 20:12 · ESV
What this means

You can honor your parents and refuse their pattern. Honor is not obedience, agreement, access, or silence. It means you do not degrade them, you do not build your identity on hating them, and you do not hand them your life as payment. If your mother failed to protect you, honoring may look like praying for her from a distance, speaking truthfully of her, and keeping safe boundaries. It is not betrayal to be the one who stopped it.

The Line Stops Here: How You Do Not Carry It On

Today’s goal

Write the promise: the line stops here.

The Bible in context · Joshua 24:15 (ESV)

Joshua 24:15 says, “And if it is disagreeable in your sight to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” Joshua says this at Shechem, near the end of his life. Notice “choose this day.” He names what came before and picks anyway.

What research suggests

Specific, written commitments with if–then plans are linked to higher follow-through. The more concrete the promise, the more likely it is to be kept.

Source: Gollwitzer, 1999. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “The line stops with me. This means ______.” Be specific (I will stay in recovery, I will get help, I will tell the truth).
  2. Write: “If I am tempted to ______, then I will ______.”
  3. Sign and date the promise.
  4. Show it to one safe person or put it where you can see it.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 6 · The Playbook and the StructureDay 56 / 90

Twelve Patterns

Today’s goal

Learn your own list of patterns, the way an investigator would.

The Bible in context · 2 Corinthians 2:11 (ESV)

Second Corinthians 2:11 says, “so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.” Paul has just urged the church to forgive and comfort a repentant man. He says being unforgiving would give Satan an advantage. Knowing the patterns of temptation and division is a defensive skill.

What research suggests

Relapse-prevention research found that identifying high-risk situations (people, places, feelings) and planning responses to them helps people avoid a lapse becoming a full relapse.

Source: Marlatt & Gordon, 1985. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. List your top three high-risk situations (for example, payday, being alone at night, arguments).
  2. Next to each write the early warning sign (a thought, a feeling, a pull).
  3. Next to each write your plan (call, leave, eat, pray).
  4. Share one with a safe person.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps

Twelve Patterns

Warfare · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 12 | Workbook 2.2
Sanctuary · optionalTake a slow sip of water. Jesus, I do not have to perform for You.
“so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.”2 Corinthians 2:11 · ESV
What this means

Volume II lays out twelve patterns that show up in the lives of people who have been hurt and stuck: being unwanted, early wounds, a false name, isolation, a coping tool, a shame loop, agreements, normalizing, passing it on, derailing the calling, waiting too long, silencing the story. This is a pattern-recognition tool, not a revealed schedule. Scripture also says much of our trouble comes from our own hearts, other people, and a broken world. Use it to notice, not to decide every hard thing was a scripted attack, and never to blame yourself for what was done to you.

Isolation: Your Family Taught You to Be Alone

Today’s goal

Reach out to one person today. Not tomorrow.

The Bible in context · Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 (ESV)

Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has not another to lift him up!” The author, called the Preacher, is looking at life under the sun and sees the cost of isolation. Companionship is described as a practical good.

What research suggests

A large analysis found that stronger social connection was associated with a substantially lower risk of death, on a scale comparable to well-known health risks. Isolation is a real risk, not just a mood.

Source: Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the name of one person you can contact (safe, even if you only know them a little).
  2. Write what you will say: “I’m having a rough day. Do you have ten minutes?”
  3. Send it now.
  4. If they do not respond, write a second name and try again.
  5. Say the declaration.

Isolation: Your Family Taught You to Be Alone

Addiction · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 12 (Stage 4), Step 24 | Workbook Part V Step 6
Sanctuary · optionalFeel your feet on the floor. Keep your eyes open. Father, meet me exactly where I am.
“Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil. For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow. But woe to him who is alone when he falls and has no one to lift him up!”Ecclesiastes 4:9-10 · ESV
What this means

Isolation makes almost every harm worse. Abusers isolate. Addiction isolates. Families that keep secrets isolate their children, and a baby who learned that no one comes may still believe it. This is why you need five kinds of people, not one: the one who knows everything, the one further ahead, the one behind you, the one who is just a friend, and the one allowed to correct you. A meeting, a sponsor, a counselor, and a church small group can fill the first of these.

Who Can Tell You You're Wrong

Today’s goal

Let someone who loves you tell you the truth.

The Bible in context · Proverbs 27:17 (ESV)

Proverbs 27:17 says, “Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another.” Verse 6 in the same chapter adds, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy.” Proverbs treats honest friends as a gift. It also assumes you pick them with care.

What research suggests

Mutual-help and peer-support groups have been shown in reviews to support recovery, partly through accountability and shared experience. Being known by people who care is protective.

Source: Kelly et al., 2020. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the name of one person who has told you the truth in love (or one you would trust to).
  2. Write one question to ask them: “What do you see that I am missing?”
  3. Ask it this week and listen without defending.
  4. Write one thing you heard and one thing you will do about it.
  5. Say the declaration.

Running Out the Clock

Today’s goal

Stop waiting for permission to start.

The Bible in context · Ephesians 5:15-16 (ESV)

Ephesians 5:15–16 says, “Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time, because the days are evil.” Paul urges careful, intentional living. “Making the best use of the time” points to seizing opportunities, not to panic.

What research suggests

Habit research shows that new behaviors become easier with daily repetition, and that missing a day here and there does not ruin the process. Starting small and starting now matters more than starting perfectly.

Source: Lally et al., 2010. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one thing you have been waiting to start (treatment, a call, a job application, a meeting, a hobby).

  3. Do that step in the next 10 minutes.
  4. Write when you will do the next step.
  5. Say the declaration.

The Trigger Chain: When Abandonment Is the Link

Today’s goal

Map one trigger chain from start to finish.

The Bible in context · 1 Peter 5:8-9 (ESV)

First Peter 5:8–9 says, “Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.” Peter writes to believers facing persecution. “Sober-minded” and “watchful” describe alert, steady attention. “Resist him, firm in your faith” puts the weight on staying planted, not on running around.

What research suggests

Research on urge surfing and mindfulness-based relapse prevention suggests that cravings rise, peak, and pass, and that noticing the process without acting can reduce relapse risk. Cravings tend to be shorter than they feel.

Source: Bowen & Marlatt, 2009. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Pick the last time you felt a strong urge or fell into an old pattern.
  2. Write the chain: What happened first? Then what did you feel? Then what did you think? Then what did you do?
  3. Circle the earliest link where you could have done something different.
  4. Write what you would do at that link next time.
  5. Say the declaration.

The Trigger Chain: When Abandonment Is the Link

Addiction · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook Part V Step 4 | Vol. II Step 27, 28
Sanctuary · optionalPut a hand on your chest and let one long breath out. Jesus, You are bigger than what I am about to read.
“Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world.”1 Peter 5:8-9 · ESV
What this means

Relapse is never one moment. It is a chain with six to ten links: the setting, the emotional state, the body, the thought, the justification, the first action, the point of no return, the use, the aftermath. For a daughter of an unprotective mother, the early links are often feeling abandoned, unseen, or dismissed, and the thought, no one cares anyway. Circle link three or four. That is where you intervene, because by link seven you had already decided.

Arc 6 · The Playbook and the StructureDay 61 / 90

HALT: Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired

Today’s goal

Run the HALT check on yourself: hungry, angry, lonely, tired.

The Bible in context · Psalm 127:2 (ESV)

Psalm 127:2 says, “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.” Psalm 127 is a song of ascents attributed to Solomon, and it opens with “Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” Rest is presented as a gift, not a weakness.

What research suggests

HALT is a recovery slogan, not a study. But the states it names (hunger, anger, loneliness, tiredness) match the kinds of situations relapse-prevention researchers describe as raising the risk of a lapse. Checking in on your basic needs is a simple, practical defense.

Source: Marlatt & Gordon, 1985. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Ask yourself four questions out loud: Am I hungry? Angry? Lonely? Tired? Say yes or no to each.
  2. Fix the first yes. Eat something with protein. Drink water. Text someone. Lie down for 20 minutes.
  3. Write what you will keep in your bag or kitchen so the first one is easy (nuts, a granola bar, water).
  4. Set one reminder on your phone at your usual low point of the day: “HALT.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps

What this means

Many relapses are several of these stacked, and they are rarely only about the substance. Lonely is the one that hits hardest for a child who was left. Some of what feels like a craving is blood sugar. Some of what feels like despair is sleep. Run the check three times a day: what is loudest, and what can I do about it in the next hour? Feed yourself, rest, call someone, calm your body. That is how you give yourself what no one gave you.

Arc 6 · The Playbook and the StructureDay 62 / 90

The Craving Wave

Today’s goal

Ride one craving wave from start to finish without acting on it.

The Bible in context · 1 Corinthians 10:13 (ESV)

First Corinthians 10:13 says, “No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” Paul is writing to a church in Corinth about Israel’s failures in the wilderness. The promise is that there is a way out, and it comes with the temptation, not after.

What research suggests

Studies of “urge surfing,” in which people notice a craving rise and fall instead of fighting or obeying it, suggest that cravings tend to peak and pass within a limited time. A mindfulness-based relapse prevention program reduced substance use over time in one large trial. These tools support treatment. They do not replace it.

Source: Bowen & Marlatt, 2009. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. When the craving hits, say, “This is a wave.” Set a timer for 10 minutes.
  2. Notice where you feel it in your body. Rate it from 0 to 10 every two minutes and write the number.
  3. Breathe in for 4, out for 6, and drink a full glass of water.
  4. When the timer ends, notice whether the number moved. Write it down.
  5. Say the declaration. If the craving is dangerous, call someone, go to a meeting, or call 988 or SAMHSA at 1-800-662-4357.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Addiction
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook Part V Step 7 | Vol. II Step 28

“No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.”1 Corinthians 10:13 · ESV
What this means

A craving often peaks and fades within fifteen to thirty minutes, even when it does not feel that way. Say it aloud: I am having a craving. It will peak and pass. Set a timer. Change your body: cold water, twenty pushups, walk outside. Change your location. Call, do not text. Eat and drink. Pray short. Play the tape forward. You only have to outlast a wave. A body that never learned to self-soothe can learn it, one wave at a time.

Play the Tape Forward: Who Else Pays

Today’s goal

Play the tape forward and see who else would pay.

The Bible in context · Proverbs 14:12 (ESV)

Proverbs 14:12 says, “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.” The verse is repeated word for word in Proverbs 16:25. Proverbs urges people to look at where a path ends, not just how it feels at the start.

What research suggests

In studies, people who were shown realistic images of their future selves made choices that favored their future more than people who were not. Seeing the end of the story makes it feel more real.

Source: Hershfield et al., 2011. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the choice you are tempted by.
  2. Write what happens in the first hour, the next day, and the next month if you do it. Be honest and specific.
  3. Write who else is affected (people, animals, your future).
  4. Write the other tape: what happens in each of those windows if you do not.
  5. Say the declaration. Read the second tape out loud.

Play the Tape Forward: Who Else Pays

Addiction · Cycle-Breaking
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook Part V Step 7 | Vol. II Step 29
Sanctuary · optionalSit with your back against something solid. Father, meet me exactly where I am.
“There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.”Proverbs 14:12 · ESV
What this means

Not the first hour. The forty-eighth. The call you would have to make. The face you would have to look at. Write it now, while you are clear, because you will not be able to write it in the moment. Arc 6 · The Playbook and the StructureDay 64 / 90

Replace the Function: What Your Mother Couldn't Give

Today’s goal

Find three better comforts for the same need.

The Bible in context · Isaiah 55:2 (ESV)

Isaiah 55:2 says, “Why do you spend your money for that which is not bread, and your labor for that which does not satisfy? Listen diligently to me, and eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food.” It is part of God’s open invitation to the thirsty to “come, buy and eat” without money. The question is about what satisfies, and it invites real nourishment.

What research suggests

Behavioral activation research suggests that adding even small, rewarding activities can lift mood over time, and that people often do not feel like doing them until after they begin. Replace a coping tool with another coping tool, not with a blank.

Source: Dimidjian et al., 2006. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. List the three moments you most reach for the old comfort (after work, at night, after conflict).
  2. Next to each write a replacement that uses a different sense: warm shower, loud song, a walk, cold water, a call, a snack, a candle.
  3. Put the replacement within reach (in your bag, on your nightstand).
  4. Use one tonight. Write how you felt after.
  5. Say the declaration.

You cannot leave a vacancy. For every job the substance did, find a legitimate replacement. It numbed pain, so find a place to put pain: therapy, a journal, a friend. It gave energy, so find food, movement, sleep. It gave belonging, so find a meeting or a church group. It quieted your head, so find music, a walk, or silence. It held you, so find real human touch, safe and chosen, and the comfort practices you are learning. God invites us to what satisfies.

Fill the House

Today’s goal

Fill one space in your home or day with something good.

The Bible in context · Romans 12:21 (ESV)

Romans 12:21 says, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” Paul has just told believers not to repay evil for evil and to live peaceably as far as it depends on them. The verse is practical: overcome by doing good, not just by avoiding the bad.

What research suggests

Research on behavioral activation and on environment design suggests that filling empty time and space with planned, meaningful activity makes old habits less automatic. Empty time is risky time.

Source: Dimidjian et al., 2006. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Pick one empty block of time (for example, Friday at 8 p.m.).
  2. Pick one good thing to put in it: a meeting, a class, a call, a walk, a craft, church, volunteering.
  3. Pick one thing in your home to change (remove something, add something: a candle, a verse, a photo of Big Boy, plants).
  4. Do the home change today.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 6 · The Playbook and the StructureDay 66 / 90

Architecture, Not Willpower

Today’s goal

Build a small daily structure that you can keep when you are tired.

The Bible in context · 1 Corinthians 14:40 (ESV)

First Corinthians 14:40 says, “But all things should be done decently and in order.” Paul is giving instructions for worship in Corinth, where meetings had become chaotic. Applied to daily life, it supports building routines. That is an application of the principle, not what the verse is directly about.

What research suggests

Habit research suggests that routines tied to a consistent place and time become more automatic, so they depend less on motivation. This is why the same wake-up, meal, and wind-down times can steady a hard season.

Source: Wood & Neal, 2007. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write a simple morning routine with only three steps (for example: water, pray two minutes, make bed).
  2. Write an evening routine with three steps (for example: dishes, shower, lights low).
  3. Put both on a card on your fridge or mirror.
  4. Do the morning routine tomorrow, even if you do not feel like it.
  5. Say the declaration.

What this means

Freedom is architecture. Same wake hour. Sunlight in the first hour. Prayer out loud. Protein and water before caffeine. Movement. A HALT check. A meeting or a call. Same bedtime, phone out of the room. Pick the three that matter most and let the others wait. If you did not grow up with structure, you are building it from scratch, and that is hard and holy. Sleep affects almost everything else.

Boundaries With Family, With Her, With Him

Today’s goal

The Bible in context · Proverbs 4:23 (ESV)

Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.” It is part of a father’s advice to his son about wisdom. Guarding the heart is described as an act of care for the source of your life, not as coldness.

What research suggests

Self-efficacy research suggests that taking small, successful actions builds confidence for larger ones. Setting and keeping a small boundary makes the next one easier.

Source: Bandura, 1977. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Arc 6 · The Playbook and the StructureDay 68 / 90

When You Fall

Today’s goal

Plan what you will do if you stumble, before you stumble.

The Bible in context · Micah 7:8 (ESV)

Micah 7:8 says, “Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.” Micah is speaking for a people who have fallen and are waiting for God to act. The verse does not say “if I never fall.” It says “when I fall, I shall rise.”

What research suggests

Relapse-prevention researchers describe the “abstinence violation effect,” where a lapse leads to shame and the thought “I have blown it,” which can lead to continued use. Planning ahead to treat a lapse as a signal instead of a verdict helps.

Source: Marlatt & Gordon, 1985. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the plan: “If I slip, I will call ______ within one hour.”
  2. Write the first three things you will do (call, leave, eat, tell, go to a meeting).
  3. Write a sentence to say to yourself instead of “I blew it”: “This is a lapse, not a life sentence.”
  4. Tell the person on your plan that they are on it.
  5. Say the declaration.

Where Was He When You Were Six Months Old?

Today’s goal

Ask the question out loud: where were you?

The Bible in context · Genesis 16:13 (ESV)

In Genesis 16 Hagar, a mistreated servant, runs into the wilderness, and the angel of the LORD finds her. She names God, “You are a God of seeing,” and says, “Truly here I have seen him who looks after me.” She is the only person in Scripture to give God a name in this way. The story does not explain her suffering. It shows that God sees her.

What research suggests

Writing honestly about painful questions, including spiritual ones, is associated in studies with modest benefits for many people. You do not need an answer to benefit from asking.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the question as plainly as you can: “God, where were you when ______?”
  2. Write what you feel when you ask it (anger, fear, numbness, hope).
  3. Read Genesis 16:7–14. Notice who sought whom.
  4. Write one sentence of what you want from God now, even if it is “I don’t know.”
  5. Say the declaration. It is okay to leave the question open.

What this means

Hagar, a mistreated servant who had run away, is the first person in Scripture to give God a name, and it is the God who sees. He was near the brokenhearted, in the room, not outside it, not arriving later. That is harder than absence, because it means He saw. It is also better than absence, because it means you were never alone, even when you felt completely alone. I do not know why He did not stop it. I know He saw, and I know He kept the record of every tear.

Why Didn't He Stop It?

Today’s goal

Let the “why didn’t he stop it” question be asked without a tidy answer.

The Bible in context · Isaiah 49:15 (ESV)

Isaiah 49:15 says, “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.” Isaiah is speaking to Zion, who had said, “The LORD has forsaken me.” God does not argue with the feeling. He says even the most unlikely forgetting will not happen to him.

What research suggests

Studies of expressive writing show that people often benefit from wrestling with painful questions on paper over several days, even without resolving them. Lament has always been a way to bring pain to God.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

“Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.”Isaiah 49:15 · ESV
What this means

God made a world with real agency, because love that cannot be refused is not love. That means people can choose evil, and He does not routinely override the will He gave. But hear how He answers in Isaiah: Can a woman forget her nursing child? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. He knows that mothers fail. And He says: I will not.

Not Punishment

Today’s goal

Separate what happened from the idea that you were being punished.

The Bible in context · John 9:3 (ESV)

In John 9:1–3 the disciples ask about a man born blind, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answers, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him.” Jesus rejects the assumption that suffering is a direct punishment for a particular sin.

What research suggests

Research on shame suggests that blaming yourself for harm done to you increases hiding and distress. Reframing responsibility accurately can reduce the weight.

Source: Tangney & Dearing, 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “I was afraid that what happened was punishment for ______.”
  2. Write the facts: who did what, and who was responsible.
  3. Write the sentence “It was not my fault” and the sentence “It was not God’s punishment.”
  4. Read John 9:1–3 aloud.
  5. Say the declaration.

Angry at God

Today’s goal

Be angry at God out loud, with the psalms to lead.

The Bible in context · Psalm 13:1-2 (ESV)

Psalm 13:1–2 says, “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day?” It is a short psalm of David. It begins in complaint and ends in trust (“I will sing to the LORD”). About a third of the psalms are laments, which means God’s own book gives you permission to be honest.

What research suggests

Writing about strong negative feelings, including anger, is linked in studies to improved well-being for many people when it moves toward meaning-making over time. Expression alone helps most when it leads somewhere.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Arc 7 · GodDay 73 / 90

Taking Your Case Out of Court

Today’s goal

Hand one case over to the only fair judge.

The Bible in context · Romans 12:19 (ESV)

Romans 12:19 says, “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.’” Paul is quoting Deuteronomy 32:35. The command is not “do nothing” in cases of abuse. Elsewhere Scripture calls on authorities to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4). It says personal revenge is not yours to carry out.

What research suggests

Studies of forgiveness programs find that people who release the desire for revenge, with support, generally report less distress. Releasing revenge does not mean the harm did not matter or that it was not a crime.

Source: Wade et al., 2014. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the name of the person and what they did, in one factual line.
  2. Write what justice would look like to you (an apology, a consequence, an acknowledgment).
  3. Decide whether any of it is something you can pursue legally or safely (a report, a restraining order, therapy). Write the next step.
  4. Pray: “God, I put this case in your hands. I will do what is mine to do.”
  5. Say the declaration.

The Quiet Stretch of Faith

Today’s goal

Sit with a quiet stretch of faith without forcing a feeling.

The Bible in context · Lamentations 3:26 (ESV)

Lamentations 3:26 says, “It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.” It sits in the middle of a poem written after the fall of Jerusalem. The author has just said, “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases,” in the midst of grief. Quiet waiting is described as good, not as failure.

What research suggests

In one study, people who walked for 90 minutes in a natural setting showed less rumination than people who walked in an urban setting. Time in quiet, green places can help a busy mind settle.

Source: Bratman et al., 2015. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Go outside, or sit by a window. Set a timer for 10 minutes.
  2. No phone. Look at one thing, like a tree or the sky.
  3. Whenever your mind runs, say “Waiting,” and look again.
  4. At the end, write one sentence about what you noticed.
  5. Say the declaration.

Arc 7 · GodDay 75 / 90

Rocked Like a Weaned Child

Today’s goal

Let yourself be quieted, like a weaned child with its mother.

The Bible in context · Psalm 131:2 (ESV)

Psalm 131:2 says, “But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.” It is a three-verse psalm of ascent attributed to David. A weaned child is not crying for milk. It simply rests. The psalmist says he has chosen not to occupy himself with things too great for him.

What research suggests

Slow breathing and gentle contact, like petting a calm animal, have both been associated with calmer physiology in studies. Neither is a cure, and both are easy to try.

Sources: Zaccaro et al., 2018; Beetz et al., 2012. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Sit or lie down with something soft, or your dog beside you.
  2. Breathe in for 4 and out for 6, ten times.
  3. Place a hand on your chest and say, “My soul is quiet. I am not in charge of everything.”
  4. Rest for three minutes without doing anything.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

Rocked Like a Weaned Child

Childhood · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 7.6 | Vol. II Ch. 27

“But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.”Psalm 131:2 · ESV
What this means

Noise was safety. If it was quiet, you could hear them coming, and you had to feel it. So silence may feel like danger before it feels like peace. Start with two minutes. Eyes open if closed feels unsafe. When your mind runs, say later and come back. The coming back is the prayer. The psalmist describes a soul quieted like a weaned child with its mother. You may not have had that mother. You can ask for it from the One who comforts like one.

Arc 7 · GodDay 76 / 90

All Things, Honestly

Today’s goal

Look at “all things work together” honestly, without calling the harm good.

The Bible in context · Romans 8:28 (ESV)

Romans 8:28 says, “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.” Paul does not say all things are good. He says God works in all things, for the good of those who love him, inside a chapter that also names suffering, groaning, and waiting. Verse 29 shows the “good” as becoming like Jesus.

What research suggests

Studies of post-traumatic growth suggest that some people report meaning and growth after trauma, and that this tends to come with, not instead of, distress. It is not required, and it is not guaranteed. In life-goal writing studies, making meaning was linked to better well-being.

Source: King, 2001. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “What happened to me was not good. It was ______.” Use real words.
  2. Write one thing God has brought you that you would not trade (a person, a lesson, a strength).
  3. Write: “I do not need to call the pain good to believe God is good.”
  4. Read Romans 8:26–28 aloud.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.

All Things, Honestly

Warfare · Cycle-Breaking
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 25 | Workbook 3.5
Sanctuary · optionalPut a hand on your chest and let one long breath out. Holy Spirit, stay near, and do not let me go further than I can hold.
“And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.”Romans 8:28 · ESV
What this means

It does not say all things are good. It says God works in all things toward good, and the next verse defines that good as being made like Christ. It is not a promise that your story will have a satisfying plot, and it is not meant to be said to someone in fresh grief. It is a promise that nothing in your story, including what happened when you were a baby and the years in your addiction, is unusable in His hands. It was not good. It will not be wasted. Those are different things.

Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 77 / 90

You Were Not Their Savior

Today’s goal

Put down the job of being everyone’s savior.

The Bible in context · Psalm 147:3 (ESV)

Psalm 147:3 says, “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” The psalm is a song of praise that celebrates God for rebuilding Jerusalem, gathering the outcasts, and healing. Healing is described as his work, not yours. The verse is a relief, not a charge.

What research suggests

Al-Anon (al-anon.org) and similar family groups exist for people affected by someone else’s drinking or drug use. They teach that you did not cause it, cannot control it, and cannot cure it, and many people find that freeing. Support groups are free.

Source: 988 Lifeline (988lifeline.org).

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the name of someone you tried to save. Write what you did to try.
  2. Write what actually happened. Be honest.
  3. Say aloud: “I did not cause it. I could not control it. I could not cure it.”
  4. Look up one family support meeting (Al-Anon, Nar-Anon, or another group) and note the time.
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps
Too much today? Stop at any step. Press your feet into the floor, name five things you can see, and reach for someone safe. Numbers are at the back.
7HE H0LY R3UP FOR ALLDay 77 · Guide
Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 77 / 90

You Were Not Their Savior

Mother Wound · Addiction
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 7.4 (Work Page 17) | Vol. II Ch. 38, 39
Sanctuary · optionalLook around until your eyes find the exit. You can leave if you need to. God, I am here. You are here. That is enough to start.
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”Psalm 147:3 · ESV
What this means

If you lost someone to addiction, you may carry the idea that you should have saved them. You may also carry it about your mother. You were not their savior. You were a child, then a sister, then a daughter, then a friend. You lost them because addiction is lethal, because they were sick, and because the world they were in was built to fail people like them. None of those were yours to control. This page is for Brandi, and for the mother you could not save. Grief is allowed here.

Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 78 / 90

Who Was Responsible

Today’s goal

Sort what was your job and what never was.

The Bible in context · Psalm 9:9 (ESV)

Psalm 9:9 says, “The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.” David praises God as the one who judges rightly and remembers the afflicted. The verse puts responsibility for justice in God’s hands, not in the hands of the victim.

What research suggests

Research on adverse childhood experiences makes the point that children are not responsible for the adversity they experience. Accurately assigning responsibility is part of healing.

Source: Felitti et al., 1998. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Make two columns: “Not my job” and “My job.”
  2. Under “Not my job” list what you were made responsible for as a child (adults’ feelings, safety, secrets, fixing).
  3. Under “My job” list what is yours now (my choices, my recovery, my relationships, my peace).
  4. Cross out one thing from your “Not my job” list that you still try to carry. Say, “I am putting this down.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps

Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 79 / 90

Hope Without Certainty

Today’s goal

Practice hope without needing certainty.

The Bible in context · Psalm 139:8 (ESV)

Psalm 139:8 says, “If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!” Sheol is the place of the dead in Hebrew thought. The psalm says there is no place so far that God is not present. It is a statement of presence, not a prediction about outcomes.

What research suggests

Writing about a hopeful but realistic future has been linked to better well-being in studies, and works best when paired with concrete steps. Hope is not a guarantee, and it is not a denial of how things are.

Source: King, 2001. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one thing you do not know and cannot know about your future.
  2. Write one thing you do know about God’s presence from Psalm 139.
  3. Write one hope you have for next year, in plain words, and one step toward it.
  4. Say, “I do not need to know how it ends to take the next step.”
  5. Say the declaration.
My notes while I do these steps

Hope Without Certainty

Warfare · Mother Wound
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 40 | Workbook 7.4
Sanctuary · optionalSit with your back against something solid. Lord, You were here before I said anything.
“If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!”Psalm 139:8 · ESV
What this means

I am not God, and I will not pretend to know where she is. But addiction is not the unforgivable sin, God judges the heart and not the manner of death (1 Samuel 16:7), and Romans 8:38-39 lists death first among the things that cannot separate us from His love. A cry does not have to be eloquent: the thief on the cross got one sentence (Luke 23:42-43). You can hope, legitimately, without lying to yourself. Hope is not certainty, and you do not need certainty to stop tormenting yourself.

Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 80 / 90

Not a Debt

Today’s goal

Receive a place in the family that is not earned.

The Bible in context · Romans 8:15 (ESV)

Romans 8:15 says, “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” Paul uses adoption language. In Roman culture an adopted son had the same legal rights as a natural child. The verse is about belonging, not debt.

What research suggests

Attachment research suggests that people who did not feel secure as children can come to feel more secure through steady relationships later, including with God, mentors, and community, although the evidence on religious attachment is still developing.

Source: Roisman et al., 2002. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “I used to think I had to earn a place by ______.”
  2. Write: “In God’s family I am a child, not a servant.”
  3. Name one place or person where you already feel you belong.
  4. Do one small thing to belong more: go to a service, a group, or a meeting.
  5. Say the declaration.

7HE H0LY R3UP FOR ALLDay 80 · Guide
Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 80 / 90

Not a Debt

Addiction · Cycle-Breaking
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Vol. II Ch. 40, 41 | Workbook 7.4
Sanctuary · optionalTake a slow sip of water. Jesus, I do not have to perform for You.
“For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"”Romans 8:15 · ESV
What this means

Their death, or their harm, did not buy your life, and there was no exchange. If you build your recovery or your work as restitution for being the one who lived, you will never be able to stop, and it will never be enough, because guilt does not close accounts. Build it because it is right, and because you love them. Their name goes on it as a dedication, not a debt. A survivor does not owe her life as payment.

The Letter: To Her, To Him, To Brandi

Today’s goal

Write the letter, to her, to him, and to Brandi, and do not mail it.

The Bible in context · John 11:35 (ESV)

John 11:35 is the shortest verse in the Bible: “Jesus wept.” It comes at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, though Jesus was about to raise him. Even knowing how the story would turn, he cried. Grief is not a lack of faith.

What research suggests

Letters you never send, a form of expressive writing, have been used in grief and trauma work and are linked in studies to emotional processing. They are most helpful when you can stop and care for yourself afterward.

Source: Pennebaker & Beall, 1986. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Pick one: a letter to the child you were, to the person who hurt you, or to Brandi Renee. Write the date at the top.
  2. Write for 15 minutes without stopping. Begin with “I need you to know.”
  3. End with one sentence of what you want to say goodbye to, or thank, or forgive.
  4. Read it aloud only if you feel steady. Then put it away. Do not mail it.
  5. Say the declaration. Do something kind for yourself afterward.

Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 82 / 90

Grief Is Not a Relapse

Today’s goal

Remember that grief is not a relapse.

The Bible in context · Matthew 5:4 (ESV)

Matthew 5:4 says, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” It is the second Beatitude, in the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus names mourning as a blessed state, because those who mourn will be met with comfort. Grief is not treated as something to hide.

What research suggests

Research on bereavement suggests people grieve in many different ways and that the most common outcome is resilience, though grief can be intense and can come in waves. Grief waves are normal, and prolonged or overwhelming grief deserves professional help.

Source: Bonanno, 2004. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write her name and dates: Brandi Renee, January 27, 1986 to December 17, 2021. Or write the name and dates of someone you have lost.
  2. Write one thing you miss and one thing you are glad you had.
  3. Light a candle or hold something of theirs for two minutes. Cry if you need to.
  4. Write: “Grief is love with nowhere to go.” Then write one place to send it today (a walk, a prayer, a kind act).
  5. Say the declaration. If grief tips toward using or self-harm, call someone or 988.

Grief that is not given a place will take one, usually as rage, shutdown, or a craving. Know your dates: birthdays, anniversaries, the day you got the call. Plan for them instead of being ambushed. Letting the Living Go: If Your Mother Is Still Here

Today’s goal

Practice gentle distance if the person is still living.

The Bible in context · Luke 5:16 (ESV)

Luke 5:16 says, “But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.” Jesus, surrounded by crowds who needed healing, regularly stepped away. It is permission to have limits and to prioritize time with the Father.

What research suggests

Self-compassion research suggests that treating your own needs as valid lowers burnout and shame. Taking space is not selfish, and it can make your care more sustainable.

Source: Neff, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write the person you need distance from or from whom you want more space.
  2. Write what you will do with the space (pray, rest, recover).
  3. Write one gentle sentence you can say: “I love you, and I need space right now.”
  4. Decide the first small step (a shorter call, a later reply, a limit on visits).
  5. Say the declaration.

Mother Wound · Warfare
Same day, other pages: Journal · Standing · Coming Home  ·  Go deeper Workbook 7.2 | Vol. II Ch. 37
Sanctuary · optionalName three things you can see and one thing you can hear. God, I am here. You are here. That is enough to start.
“But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.”Luke 5:16 · ESV
What this means

There are four kinds of letting go: release to God with them still in your life, boundary, distance, and no contact. You are not obligated to give unlimited access to someone who is actively harming you, and no Scripture requires it. If your mother is living, decide which kind fits now and what would change it. If she is gone, you may still be letting go of the mother you needed and the apology you may never hear. You can love someone and not be their savior.

Arc 8 · Brandi and Letting GoDay 84 / 90

The Release

Today’s goal

Release what you cannot carry.

The Bible in context · Psalm 55:22 (ESV)

Psalm 55:22 says, “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.” David wrote this in distress over betrayal by a close friend. “Cast” is a physical word, like throwing something off your back. The promise is that God sustains, not that the burden vanishes instantly.

What research suggests

Naming heavy feelings in words has been linked to reduced intensity of emotional reactions in lab studies. Naming each burden before you hand it over can make the handing-over more real.

Source: Lieberman et al., 2007. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write three burdens you are still carrying, in a line each.
  2. Next to each write: “I cannot fix this.”
  3. Hold a heavy object (a book, a bag of rice). Say, “I cast this on you, Lord.” Put it down.
  4. Notice the lightness in your hands. Take three breaths.
  5. Say the declaration.

Known Before You Were Formed

Today’s goal

Believe that you were known and wanted before you were hurt.

The Bible in context · Psalm 139:13-14 (ESV)

Psalm 139:13–14 says, “For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother’s womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.” David wrote this as a song of praise. The verse says that God was involved in your making, no matter what the circumstances of your birth or your parents’ choices were.

What research suggests

Studies on self-compassion suggest that seeing yourself as worthy of care, not because of achievement, is linked to better emotional health. Worth is not something you have to prove.

Source: Neff, 2003. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write: “Before anything happened, God made me. He saw me as ______.”
  2. Write three things about yourself that you like or that make you you (your laugh, your grit, your love for animals).
  3. Look in the mirror and say, “I am fearfully and wonderfully made,” once.
  4. Write one thing you would like to say to the child who was hurt: “You were wanted by God.”
  5. Say the declaration.

The Wound as a Door

Today’s goal

Notice that your wound can become a door for someone else.

The Bible in context · 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 (ESV)

Second Corinthians 1:3–4 says, “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” Paul wrote it after severe hardship in Asia. Comfort is received so it can be passed on. It does not say your pain was good, only that it can be used.

What research suggests

In a study of people in alcohol recovery, those who helped other people in Alcoholics Anonymous were more likely to stay sober over the following year than those who did not. Helping from a place of stability seems to benefit the helper as well.

Source: Pagano et al., 2004. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write one lesson from your journey that someone else could use.
  2. Write who might need it (a newcomer in a meeting, a friend, a younger woman).
  3. Write one safe way to share it (a text, a meeting share, a card).
  4. Only share what is stable and healed enough for you. You are not required to reopen anything.
  5. Say the declaration.

Today’s goal

The Bible in context · John 15:16 (ESV)

John 15:16 says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.” Jesus says this to the disciples at the Last Supper, in the passage about the vine and the branches. “Appointed” and “bear fruit” mean you are chosen for something, but the fruit comes from staying connected to him.

What research suggests

Self-efficacy research suggests that imagining and practicing the person you want to be, then taking small steps that match, builds confidence over time. Identity is built by actions.

Source: Bandura, 1977. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Two Roads: Carrying It On, or Ending It Here

Today’s goal

Choose between carrying it on and ending it here, and write the choice.

The Bible in context · Deuteronomy 30:19 (ESV)

Deuteronomy 30:19 says, “I call heaven and earth to witness against you today, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live.” Moses is speaking to Israel at the end of his life. The choice is repeated, and it is presented as real, with help from God (v. 20).

What research suggests

Specific, written plans are linked to higher follow-through. A choice you have written and told someone about is more likely to hold.

Source: Gollwitzer, 1999. Full citations are in the back of the book.

  2. Write: “Ending it here looks like ______.” Be specific.

  4. Tell one safe person your three actions.
  5. Say the declaration.

Steward, Not Survivor: What You Pass On Without Children

Today’s goal

Plan what you will pass on without having children.

The Bible in context · 2 Timothy 1:5 (ESV)

Second Timothy 1:5 says, “I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.” Paul writes to Timothy, his spiritual son. Faith was passed through relationship. Paul himself had no biological children and passed faith on through discipleship.

What research suggests

Studies on “future self continuity” suggest that feeling connected to your future self helps with long-term choices. Legacy is a way of caring for the people who will come after you, including your future self.

Source: Hershfield et al., 2011. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Write who you could pass something on to (a niece, a mentee, a younger friend, a neighbor, a newcomer in recovery).
  2. Write what you want to pass on (a recipe, a skill, a verse, a boundary, a way to ask for help).
  3. Write one small act this month (a coffee, a card, a call).
  4. Do it or schedule it.
  5. Say the declaration.

Cycle-Breaking · Warfare

“I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.”2 Timothy 1:5 · ESV
What this means

Victim: this happened to me. Survivor: and I am still here. Steward: and now it belongs to God and it is for somebody else. You do not need children to pass something on. You pass it on to the people who watch how you live: friends, nieces, nephews, coworkers, people in a meeting, people you mentor. Paul remembered a line of faith that passed through women, a grandmother and a mother. You can start a line of faith and honesty, whether or not you ever raise a child. What you pass on is how you live.

The Commission

Today’s goal

Close the ninety days by commissioning yourself, honestly and with a next step.

The Bible in context · Nehemiah 4:14 (ESV)

Nehemiah 4:14 says, “And I looked and arose and said to the nobles and to the officials and to the rest of the people, ‘Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes.’” Nehemiah is rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem under threat. The people worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, and they finished.

What research suggests

Habit research suggests new behaviors can take around two months or more to become automatic, and that missing days does not undo progress. Writing about your future in a realistic way is associated with better well-being.

Sources: Lally et al., 2010; King, 2001. Full citations are in the back of the book.

Do this, step by step about 15 minutes · check each box
  1. Look back through your ninety days. Write three things that changed.
  2. Write one practice you will keep (morning armor, craving surfing, HALT, a daily call, a meeting).
  3. Write one thing you will do in the next thirty days to build on this.
  4. Write a short commission to yourself: “I am ______. I am here to ______.”
  5. Say the declaration. Tell one person what you finished.

The Challenge Jar§H61§

Cut along the dashed lines, fold each card, and keep them in a jar or envelope. Draw one at random any time — when a day feels flat, when it feels too heavy, or when you finish early. Use as many or as few as you like.

Day 87–90

A Letter From Her§H62§

Write as the girl at the doorway. Let her say what she has wanted to say. She can be angry, tender, funny, or quiet. You do not have to edit her.

Day 88–90

A Letter From the New Me§H63§

Write as the woman you are becoming: “I am here now. I am safe. I will not leave you. Here is what I promise.” Be specific and kind.

Day 90

Our Promise§H64§

Read both letters aloud, then write one promise you can keep, small enough to do on a bad day.

Signed: ____________________________________   Date: ____ / ____ / ________

Witnessed by: ____________________________________

Welcome home. We are a team. We are not finished, and we are not alone.

Looking back

Final Reflection§H50§

Take your time. Answer in pencil if that feels safer. You are not grading yourself — you are noticing.

What is one thing I told the truth about that I had been avoiding?

Where did I feel the most resistance, and what might that be protecting?

What is one thing that is different — even slightly — from when I started?

What do I still need help with, and who could I ask?

Fill this in honestly. “Still hard” is an allowed answer. Finishing is not the same as being finished.

Your next step

Next-Step Challenge§H52§

Go back to Day 1 and read what you wrote — not to grade yourself, to see it. Then choose one practice (the armor, the craving protocol, the silence, the release) and keep it for the next thirty days. Tell one person which one.

My one next step

Who will know about it, and by when?

What will I do if I miss a day?

Pick the page back up. Missing a day is not failure — the identity is in the rising.

Closing Prayer

Father, thank You for walking with me through these pages. I did not do this perfectly, and You never asked me to. Where I told the truth, thank You for staying. Where I skipped, meet me there with patience. Where I found grief, hold me in it. Where I found anger, let me bring it to You instead of away from You. Give me safe people, good help, and a next step small enough to take. Keep me honest without letting me shame myself. Teach me to tend what You have given me — slowly, the way a vineyard is tended. I belong to You, and I am still building. In Jesus' name. Amen.

Keep this page

Help, Right Now§H54§

If you are in danger right now, or the thought of dying has teeth in it today, stop reading and call. That is not failure. That is the correct use of this page.

NeedContact
988 Suicide & Crisis LifelineCall or text 988 · free, 24/7, confidential
Crisis Text LineText HOME to 741741
SAMHSA National Helpline (substance use, treatment referrals)1-800-662-4357 · free, 24/7, confidential
National Domestic Violence Hotline1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788
RAINN (sexual assault)1-800-656-4673
National Human Trafficking Hotline1-888-373-7888, or text 233733
Veterans Crisis LineDial 988, then press 1

Good to know

  • Narcan (naloxone) is available without an individual prescription at most pharmacies, and free through many health departments and harm-reduction programs. Keep it in the house even if you do not use. It can reverse an opioid overdose and will not hurt someone who did not take opioids.
  • Withdrawal from alcohol, benzodiazepines, and barbiturates can kill you. Do not detox from those alone. That is a medical detox, not a willpower problem. Call SAMHSA or go to an emergency room.
  • Numbers and services change. Confirm them before you rely on them.
